v001.objective: Open the batch's first lesson: name what Legal Support Help does, and that from today everything they do is a law firm's work product.
talk: Welcome the batch by name and say which lesson this is — Lesson 1, VA Essentials.
Two things carry through all 18 days: accuracy and confidentiality. Everything after this builds on them.
Housekeeping: cameras on for discussions, type 'done' in the GC at the end of every task, and all submissions go to their own Assessments/Activities folder.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day, everyone! Welcome to Day 1 of your Foundational Training. 😊

Kindly proceed right away to your first set of tasks for today's session. Thank you.

Topics: Common Terms Used & Auto Liability Insurance

Reminders for the whole training:
• Type "done" here in the GC after every task.
• Save every output in your own Assessments/Activities folder.
• Follow the file naming convention given for each task — the name is part of the grade.

keys: Tools they must have working today: Smart Advocate (SA) access, Nitro Pro (or another PDF editor that merges and edits text), Microsoft Word, Notepad.
SECURITY SOP: SA is on the 2nd password during training shifts and goes back to the 1st password at end of shift. VAs never change this password themselves.
pitfalls: Trainees who 'watch' with no notes — tell them now that the monitoring sheet items are graded.
Someone missing a tool. Settle it today, not on a demo day.

v002.objective: Set the bar: by the end they support a U.S. firm professionally — not just finish tasks.
talk: Read the objective, then put it in their words: structure, operations and expectations of U.S. law firms.
Point out what is coming: legal practice, firm types, areas of law, clientele, U.S. time zones and states, cultural context, the legal system, key terminology.
Say plainly that every item on that list shows up in a graded activity later.
pitfalls: Treating the objective slide as a formality. Ask one person to say it back before moving on.

v003.objective: Give them the map of the lesson so they can see where each part lands.
talk: Walk the agenda top to bottom, one line each — do not teach it here.
Flag the two items that become homework tonight: Common Terms and Auto Liability Insurance.
pitfalls: Teaching the agenda. It is a map; the parts come later.

v004.objective: Make cultural alignment concrete: U.S. legal culture, deadlines, confidentiality and tone are the job, not background.
talk: Professionalism, proactivity and cultural awareness are what get a VA kept on a firm.
Anticipating a need beats waiting to be told — that is the difference between hours renewed and a project ended.
Confidentiality is covered properly in Lesson 2, but it starts today.
pitfalls: Hearing 'cultural awareness' as accent training. It is deadlines, directness, and knowing what may not be said.

v020.objective: Place the Legal VA in the firm: a skilled remote professional, from admin through legal research.
talk: Why firms hire VAs: streamline operations, raise efficiency, keep attorney hours on legal work.
A Legal VA is not a generic VA — the work is file work on live cases.
pitfalls: Thinking 'virtual' means informal. The output is a law firm's work product either way.

v021.objective: Show the trade the firm is making: routine work moves to the VA so lawyers keep case preparation and client communication.
talk: Scheduling, email, documents — those are the routine tasks that come across.
Everything they take off the attorney's desk has to come back right the first time; a correction costs the firm more than the task saved.
pitfalls: Assuming routine means low stakes. A missed calendar entry is a missed deadline.

v022.objective: Benefits 1 and 2 — efficiency and cost — from the firm's side of the table.
talk: Efficiency: a skilled VA finishes faster and more accurately than an untrained in-house hire.
Cost: no benefits, no office space, no equipment for the firm.
Say the consequence: they are being paid for throughput and accuracy, and both are measured.

v023.objective: Benefits 3 and 4 — specialized skills and flexibility.
talk: Specialized skills: legal research, document preparation, transcription — this is why the 18 days exist.
Flexibility: VAs often cover outside traditional business hours, and U.S. time zones are the reason.
pitfalls: Hearing 'flexibility' as 'no fixed schedule'. Shifts are set; coverage is the point.

v024.objective: Benefit 5 — better client service, because attorneys get their time back.
talk: The client feels the VA's work even when the client never speaks to the VA.
Whether a VA may speak to clients at all is firm policy — that comes back in the Lesson 2 scenarios.

v025.objective: Open Tasks and Roles: firms run from one attorney to multi-state organizations, and handle nearly every kind of matter.
talk: Everything in this part answers one question for them: what will I actually be asked to do?
Tell them the five scenarios are coming and will be graded on reasoning, not on guessing the label.

v026.objective: Separate Legal Assistant from Paralegal cleanly.
talk: Both support the practice; the duties differ.
Our VAs work the Legal Assistant side of that line unless a firm says otherwise.
keys: Legal Assistant — administrative support: calendars, documents, file upkeep, financial and operational tasks.
Paralegal — substantive legal work delegated by an attorney: research, drafting pleadings, discovery; works under attorney supervision.
Neither may give legal advice. That line is absolute.
pitfalls: Using the titles interchangeably on a call with a client or a provider.

v027.objective: Make the Legal Assistant's day concrete, and note how close it sits to a legal secretary's.
talk: Appointments, document preparation, financial and operational tasks.
Ask the room which of those they have done in any job — most have done all of them, just not on a case file.

v028.objective: State the hinge of this part: the type of firm changes the job and the environment.
talk: Same title, different firm, different day. Keep this in mind for the scenarios.

v029.objective: Give the range — solo attorney up to multi-state, hundreds of staff.
talk: Size drives how specialized or how broad their work will be.

v030.objective: Tie task mix to firm type before naming the four categories.
talk: The kind of work follows the kind of firm. Nobody chooses their task mix; the firm's structure does.

v031.objective: Land the four task categories, then run the first two Practical Application scenarios against them.
talk: Transactional, Client-Centric, All-Around, Departmentalized — define each in one line.
Run Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 here. Make them justify the answer before you confirm it.

gc.label: Scenarios 1 and 2
gc.text:
PRACTICAL APPLICATION — Tasks and Roles
What type of Legal VA task category does each belong to? (Transactional / Client-Centric / All-Around / Departmentalized)

Scenario 1: A VA is asked to send a settlement breakdown today, and tomorrow to organize medical records.

Scenario 2: A VA works only in the medical records department, retrieving records daily.

Type your answer here with one sentence of reasoning. Thank you.

keys: Scenario 1 — Transactional Tasks. Different discrete task each day, no single owned function.
Scenario 2 — Departmentalized Tasks. One department, one repeated function, daily.
Transactional = task-by-task. Client-Centric = owns the client relationship. All-Around = everything, usually solo/small. Departmentalized = one function inside a larger firm.
pitfalls: Calling Scenario 1 'All-Around' — All-Around is about breadth of role in a small firm, not a different task each day.
Answering with the label alone. The reasoning is what is graded.

match: Scenario 1: "Transactional"
Scenario 2: "Departmentalized"
reasoning mentions varied/different tasks per day (S1)
reasoning mentions one department / single repeated function (S2)
nlp: Accept semantic equivalents: 'task-based', 'per-task', 'one-off tasks' for Transactional; 'specialized to one unit', 'records department only' for Departmentalized.
Score label and reasoning separately — a right label with absent or wrong reasoning caps at 50% for that scenario.
Reject answers that name two categories without choosing one.

rubric: Answered in own words, not read from the slide
Spoke up without being called on
trainer.feedback: What their reasoning showed about how they read a task list…

v032.objective: Smaller firms need multi-skilled VAs — that is how hours get built.
talk: In a small firm there is little to delegate, so range is what earns hours.
This is the setup for Scenario 3; do not give that answer away yet.

v033.objective: Name the consequence honestly — a VA judged unskilled loses hours or the project — then run Scenario 3.
talk: Say it straight: the firm's alternative is to work alone. Hours are not guaranteed.
Run Scenario 3 on the solo attorney practice.

gc.label: Scenario 3
gc.text:
PRACTICAL APPLICATION — Scenario 3
You are assigned to a solo attorney practice. The attorney asks you to answer calls, organize files, schedule appointments, and send billing follow-ups.

Question: What does this tell you about the type of law firm and your expected role?

Type your answer here. Thank you.

keys: Scenario 3 — a Small Law Firm or Solo Practice, and an All-Around role: one VA covering reception, files, calendar and billing follow-up.
Strong answers also say why: there is no department to hand work to.
pitfalls: Naming only the role or only the firm type. The question asks for both.

match: "Solo" or "Solo Practice" or "Small Law Firm"
"All-Around" role
at least two of: calls, files, scheduling, billing
nlp: Accept 'one-person firm', 'single attorney' for Solo; 'generalist', 'wears many hats' for All-Around.
Require both the firm type and the role for full marks.

rubric: Connected it to their own expected workload
trainer.feedback: Notes on how they read the firm from the task list…

v034.objective: Large firms move people between roles; comfort with that transfer is the requirement.
talk: A transfer out of intake into medical records is normal, not a demotion.
Setup for Scenario 4 — restructuring.

v035.objective: Close Tasks and Roles with the flexibility point, then run Scenarios 4 and 5.
talk: When a firm struggles, it keeps the VAs who have handled more than one role.
Run Scenario 4 (restructuring) and Scenario 5 (client communication restriction) back to back — they both come down to adapting to the firm's SOP.

gc.label: Scenarios 4 and 5
gc.text:
PRACTICAL APPLICATION — Scenarios 4 and 5

Scenario 4: You were originally assigned to the intake department, but the law firm later transferred you to medical records because another department needed support.
Question: Why does this happen, and what quality is the firm looking for?

Scenario 5: At one law firm, VAs are not allowed to communicate directly with clients, but at another firm they are allowed to follow up with clients regarding documents.
Question: What lesson should a Legal VA learn from this?

Type your answers here. Thank you.

keys: Scenario 4 — larger firms restructure departments by workload and staffing. Qualities sought: high flexibility, strong adaptability, proactive willingness to learn new tasks.
Scenario 5 — every firm has different policies and workflows. Adapt to the client's SOP, follow their rules, never assume procedures are the same across firms.
SOP ADHERENCE is the takeaway of this whole part: the firm's rule wins over what we were taught elsewhere.
pitfalls: Reading Scenario 4 as unfair treatment.
Answering Scenario 5 with 'both are fine' — the lesson is to follow the SOP of the firm you are on, and to verify before acting.

match: S4: "restructure" / workload / staffing needs
S4: "flexibility" AND "adaptability"
S5: "SOP"
S5: 'never assume' / policies differ per firm
nlp: Accept 'reorganize', 'reassign', 'department needs' for restructuring; 'willing to learn' counts toward adaptability.
S5 full marks require both: policies differ by firm AND the VA follows the client's SOP.
Flag any answer that says a VA may decide for themselves whether to contact a client — that is a hard fail on this item.

rubric: Asked what to do when an SOP is unclear
trainer.feedback: Notes on their attitude to reassignment and to firm rules…

v036.objective: Solo firms: one lawyer, often outside paralegals, personal attention, one or two focus areas.
talk: Solo practitioners may be new or very experienced — do not assume either.
For a VA: broadest role, closest contact with the attorney, least backup.
keys: Solo = 1 attorney. May hire outside paralegals and experts. General or specialized. VA role: All-Around.

v037.objective: Small / boutique firms: 2–10 attorneys, close collaboration, limited resources.
talk: Boutique means highly specialized and personalized, not small-time.
Limited resources mean more administrative load on the lawyers — which is exactly where the VA is used.
keys: Small/boutique = 2–10 attorneys. Autonomy, broad legal topics, resource constraints. VA role: All-Around to Transactional.

v038.objective: Medium firms: 50 to several hundred attorneys, partner-level service with real staffing behind it.
talk: Less prestige than large, more autonomy and a more strategic case load.
For a VA: departments start to exist, so work narrows.
keys: Medium = 50–several hundred attorneys. VA role: Departmentalized or Client-Centric.

v039.objective: Large firms: hundreds to thousands of attorneys, offices nationwide and abroad, fast and complex work.
talk: The largest U.S. firms run upward of 3,000 attorneys.
For a VA: narrow function, high volume, strict process — and transfers between departments, as in Scenario 4.
keys: Large = several hundred to thousands of attorneys, multi-office, multi-state and international. VA role: strictly Departmentalized.
pitfalls: Assuming large firms mean more interesting work. It usually means one slice of the process, done exactly to SOP.

v134.objective: Tips 1 and 2 — own the case management system, and account for time like a lawyer.
talk: Master the CMS: shortcuts, tagging, pulling reports and tasks. Self-sufficiency is the value.
Think like a lawyer: time is the firm's product. Log entries clearly and specifically.
keys: Our CMS in training is Smart Advocate (SA). From Lesson/Day 9 onward every demo is scored inside SA.
A good time entry names the system, the party and the task: 'Updated Clio with billing from OrthoSouth — 15 mins'.
pitfalls: Vague time entries ('worked on case'). They are unbillable and they get noticed.

v135.objective: Tips 3 and 4 — be proactive, and keep written communication clean.
talk: Proactive means anticipating the next step: the IME is scheduled, so offer the transport request.
Clear subject lines and bullet points. 'RECORDS REQUEST: OrthoSouth — Smith, John' tells the reader everything before they open it.
keys: Subject-line pattern used throughout this training: [Client Name] - [Entity] - [Type of Request].
pitfalls: Proactive is not acting outside authority. Offer, then wait for the go-ahead.

v136.objective: Tips 5 and 6 — know the PI process, and keep learning past the task list.
talk: The phases: intake → treatment → demand → negotiation → settlement. This is the spine of the whole program.
Tell them this exact lifecycle is the first Process Question on Reception day, and they will be asked what a VA does at each stage.
keys: PI case lifecycle: Intake → Treatment → Demand → Negotiation → Settlement.
Roles against the phases: Reception and Intake at the front, Claims and Provider Communication through treatment, Lien Negotiator after settlement.
pitfalls: Memorizing the five words without the VA tasks attached to each.

v137.objective: The mindset page — read it as a standard, not a poster.
talk: Precision, purpose, professionalism. Anticipate, act, lead quietly.
Close on the one that is graded every day: bring clarity, calm and confidence to every case you touch.
pitfalls: Rushing past it. This is the page to come back to when a trainee's attitude slips in week two.

v138.objective: Close the lesson and set tonight's homework: both assessments, plus monitoring items #5–7.
talk: Confirm both videos are watched and both reference files are open.
Give the homework, the folder and the deadline in one message, then take questions.
While they wait for their teammates, point them at the supplementary Personal Injury articles.

v001.objective: Open Law Firm Communication: every call a VA takes or makes is the firm speaking.
talk: Frame the day: softphones, call handling, and who we are allowed to say what to.
Tell them the afternoon is a breakout — Process Questions and the escalation exercise — so they listen for the answers now.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting our classroom discussion on Law Firm Communication.

Topics: Softphones · Call Handling · Law Firm Call Management · Attorney-Client Privilege

This afternoon (1:00–3:00 PM) we go into breakout for the Process Questions and the Escalation Handling exercise. Please take notes as we go — the answers come from this discussion. Thank you.

pitfalls: Trainees treating this as a soft topic. It is the one lesson where a mistake is a legal exposure, not a rework.

v004.objective: Name the first half: inbound calls — calls that come to the firm.
talk: Inbound is reception's world: whoever picks up decides what happens to that caller.
Tell them the ten inbound habits are each one page, and the first five decide whether the caller stays.

v005.objective: Separate the three inbound roles so they know which hat they are wearing.
talk: Receptionist, Intake Specialist, Appointment Setter — one caller can pass through all three.
Our program trains all three: Reception on Days 3–4, Intake from Day 7, Calendaring on Days 5–6.
keys: Receptionist — greets, screens, triages, transfers, documents.
Intake Specialist — qualifies the lead, asks the intake questions, collects the documents.
Appointment Setter — confirms availability and plots the attorney's calendar.

v006.objective: Show what reception intake really decides: whether this is a good lead.
talk: Determining a good lead is a judgement made in the first minute, on the intake questions.
A bad screen costs the attorney a consultation slot; a missed good lead costs the firm a case.
pitfalls: Screening by how upset the caller is rather than by the facts of the matter.

v010.objective: Tone is the first impression — and it is role-specific. Start building the tone matrix here.
talk: Callers can hear a smile; they can also hear impatience. Calm and clarity are the default.
Start the tone matrix now and finish it on the court/adjuster/opposing-counsel pages: the tone changes with who is on the line, the facts never do.
keys: TONE MATRIX (used in the Process Questions and the Day 4 mock calls):
Worried client — warm, patient, reassuring; no promises about outcome or value.
Insurance adjuster — neutral, brief, factual; share only what is allowed.
Court staff — formal, precise, deferential; case number and case style ready.
Opposing counsel — correct and minimal; never volunteer anything.
Medical provider — professional and cooperative; public information only.
pitfalls: One tone for everyone. A client tone with an adjuster leaks; an adjuster tone with a client sounds cold.

v011.objective: Script plus tone is what makes a hard call (past-due invoices) survivable.
talk: The script carries compliance; the tone carries the relationship. They need both.
This is Process Question 4 — scripted versus freeform. Let them hear the answer forming here.
keys: Scripted calls win on professionalism and compliance: nothing is improvised that could mislead or disclose.
Freeform wins on rapport — so the answer is a script as the floor, with the VA's own words on top, never instead.

v022.objective: Documentation is part of the call, not paperwork after it.
talk: Document to the firm's preferred method: email, call log, CRM note.
If it is not in the CMS, it did not happen. From Day 9 they do this in Smart Advocate for real.
keys: Every note names: who called, what they wanted, what was said, what happens next, and who owns the next step.
pitfalls: Writing notes from memory at the end of the shift.
Notes that record the VA's opinion of the caller rather than the facts.

v037.objective: Provider calls: public information only — and this is where the privilege line gets tested.
talk: Name, phone number, address: public. Anything else, stop.
Some providers will ask for private information. The answer is that we will send it through the authorized request, not read it out.
keys: Confidential information — anything we learn about the client's matter; protected by duty.
Privileged communication — communication between client and attorney for legal advice; protected from disclosure altogether.
This distinction is Process Question 3, and it is the one trainees most often get wrong.
pitfalls: Reading out a date of birth or SSN because the person on the line sounds official.

v040.objective: Adjuster calls: the guardrails, before anyone practises one.
talk: Put the two lists on the board before the script. They matter more than the wording.
This is the same rule they will use on Day 10 when opening claims.
keys: DO NOT SHARE with an adjuster: Date of Birth, Email address, SSN, VIN.
MAY SHARE: client's first and last name (no middle name), vehicle information such as the plate number, city and state only, and the law firm's phone number.
Why it is safe: those items are already in the police report the adjuster has.
pitfalls: Giving the client's own phone number instead of the firm's.
Confirming a detail the adjuster reads out — confirming is disclosing.

v045.objective: Court calls: formal, prepared, and never substantive.
talk: Confirm the department first, then give the case number and case style.
Court staff are not a source of advice and we do not argue the matter with them.
keys: Have ready before dialling: case number, case style, attorney's name, the specific ask.
pitfalls: Calling the court without the case number in front of them.

v048.objective: Opposing counsel: correct, minimal, and nothing volunteered.
talk: Identify the firm, make the single request, confirm what was agreed, end the call.
Never discuss the facts, the treatment, the demand or the client's situation — not even to be helpful.
keys: A voicemail to opposing counsel carries name, firm, callback number and the subject only — never case details.
pitfalls: Being drawn into small talk about the case. That is the most common real-world leak.

grade.deliverable: Entity communication matrix — who may be told what

match: Adjuster: DOB, email, SSN, VIN listed as never shared
Adjuster: name, plate, city/state, firm phone listed as shareable
Provider: public information only
Opposing counsel: no case details, no volunteered information
Court: case number and case style
nlp: Score per entity; a correct rule for one entity does not carry to another.
Treat 'I would check with the attorney first' as a correct answer where the item is not on the allowed list.
Any answer that permits sharing SSN, DOB, email or VIN with an adjuster is a hard fail regardless of composite score.

rubric: Professional deference — defers to attorney rather than guessing
Holds the line politely under pressure
Phone etiquette: identifies firm, confirms, closes
trainer.feedback: How they held the line when the caller pushed…

v053.objective: Close outbound with the preparation habit: name, number, purpose and documents before dialling.
talk: Prepared calls are short calls. Unprepared calls are the ones that need a second call.
Double-check everything, and have the note half-written before the phone rings.

v024.objective: Name the second half: outbound — the firm reaching out, where who we are calling changes everything.
talk: Five audiences: clients, invoices, providers, adjusters, court and opposing counsel.
Each has its own script and its own limit on what may be said.

v054.objective: Close the deck, then run the breakout: handouts, Process Questions, the escalation exercise, and tonight's homework.
talk: Post the four handouts, then split the group.
Run the five Priority questions if time is short; the full eleven if the batch is moving well.
Finish with the Escalation Handling exercise, then give the homework.

match: File name matches the convention exactly, with the trainee's first name

v002.objective: The objective: clarity, confidentiality and effectiveness on every call.
talk: Three words to hold the whole lesson against. Each one is a scored metric later.

v003.objective: The agenda: softphones, call handling, law firm call management.

v007.objective: Answer within the first ring — and what that signals.
talk: Speed is the first thing a caller judges. It costs nothing and it is noticed.

v008.objective: First impressions form in the first seven seconds to two minutes.
talk: If most of that is hold music, the impression is already made.
pitfalls: Answering and then immediately asking the caller to hold while the CMS loads.

v009.objective: Be ready: adapt to any call in real time.
talk: Hesitation reads as inexperience even when the answer is right. Preparation removes it.

v012.objective: Hold time is a last resort.
talk: Offer a callback instead of a long hold when research is needed.
keys: If it will take more than a moment: take the number, give a time, and call back inside it.

v013.objective: Ask permission before a hold or a transfer, and say why.
talk: Permission, reason, reassurance — in that order, every time.

v014.objective: Make the caller feel valued: personalise it.
talk: Use their name, acknowledge what they came for, and do not rush them off.

v015.objective: Stay mindful and respectful — you never know what will land badly.
talk: Neutral, professional language. No humour about the case, the injury or the delay.

v016.objective: Be consistent: inconsistency invites questions you cannot answer.
talk: Two different answers from two VAs costs the firm its credibility on that file.

v017.objective: Admit what you do not know rather than guessing.
talk: Then promise the follow-up and own it. That is the whole trust mechanism.
keys: Line to use: 'I don't want to give you the wrong information — let me check and come back to you by [time].'

v018.objective: Stay in control of the conversation while staying friendly.
talk: Friendly and in control are not in tension. Letting a call wander is what loses both.

v019.objective: Own the call: be a responsible, well-guided point of contact.

v020.objective: Recap at the end: summarise the key points.
talk: It catches errors and it tells the caller they were heard.

v021.objective: The after-call summary, and documenting it accurately.

v023.objective: Taking notes and updating records during the call.
talk: Across several clients and matters, the note written during the call is the only reliable one.

v025.objective: Common outbound: follow-ups on treatment, case status, consultations.
talk: Each follow-up has a purpose. Name it before dialling.

v026.objective: Appointment reminders — and everything a reminder must include.
talk: Facility name, kind of appointment, time, address. Missing one makes the reminder useless.
keys: Reminder must carry: facility, type of appointment, date and time, and the address.

v027.objective: Client contact calls: greet, introduce the firm, authenticate.
talk: Authentication on an outbound call too — we called them, but we still confirm who we have.

v028.objective: State the purpose clearly and ask the relevant questions.
talk: Listen rather than racing the client through a list.

v029.objective: Thank them, and leave a voicemail if needed.
talk: A voicemail to a client carries name, firm, callback and a reason — never case detail.

v030.objective: Invoice follow-up: greet, introduce, confirm you have the client.
talk: Money calls need the identity confirmed before anything else is said.

v031.objective: Confirm they received the invoice email; offer payment help or a plan.
talk: Offer, never pressure. A payment plan is the firm's to approve.

v032.objective: The sample script — read it as written, then have a trainee read it back.

v033.objective: The variant script for when it is not the client on the line.
talk: Nothing about the balance is said to anyone but the client.

v034.objective: Document every call on the CRM, with the template given.
talk: Use the template as-is. Consistent notes are what make a file readable by the next person.

v035.objective: The email template: reply on the existing REMINDER thread.
talk: Replying on the thread keeps the history in one place and the cc list right.

v036.objective: Provider calls: greet, introduce, confirm the right contact person.
talk: The records department, by name, is usually who they actually need.

v038.objective: The provider sample script — the records and billing follow-up.

v039.objective: Thank them; leave a voicemail if necessary.

talk: Short, factual and within the guardrails on the earlier page.

v043.objective: Voicemail to an adjuster: name, brief reason, callback time and number.
talk: Brief reason means the subject, not the facts.
pitfalls: Leaving case detail on an adjuster's voicemail.

v044.objective: The adjuster sample script — following up on a liability decision.

v046.objective: Court calls: give the case number and case style, then thank them.
talk: Both identifiers, ready before dialling.

v047.objective: The court sample script — coordinating a hearing.

v049.objective: Opposing counsel: confirm what was gathered, give the case reference.
talk: Confirming avoids a second call. It is not an invitation to discuss.

v050.objective: Voicemail to opposing counsel: never provide case information.
talk: Name, firm, callback, subject. Nothing else, ever.
Then close the outbound run on the best-practices page.

v001.objective: Open the PI Workflow deck: the one map the rest of the 18 days hangs on.
talk: Tell them plainly: every role they will train for sits somewhere on this map.
By the end of this deck they must be able to name the stages in order, unprompted.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting our classroom discussion on the Personal Injury Workflow.

By the end of this part you should be able to name the stages of a PI case in order, and say what a Legal VA does at each one. Please take notes — this is the first Process Question. Thank you.

pitfalls: Trainees who know PI from another firm and assume the stages are named the same. Use our stage names.

v002.objective: Set the frame: every claim turns on its own facts, and PI law decides who can be claimed against.
talk: No two claims are identical — which is why SOP matters more than memory.
PI law governs what creates grounds for a claim and who the claim can be made against.

v003.objective: The stage list — have them write it down before anything is explained.
talk: Read the stages in order, then have the room say them back without the slide.
Mark where each specialist role lives: Reception and Intake at the front, Claims at set-up, Provider Communication through treatment and records, Lien Negotiator after settlement.
keys: Legal Intake and Consultation → Claims Set-Up and Liability Determination → Treatment → Collecting Medical Bills and Records → Demand → Negotiation → Settlement and Disbursement (→ Litigation where no settlement is reached).
The short form used elsewhere in this program: Intake → Treatment → Demand → Negotiation → Settlement.
pitfalls: Putting Demand before records are collected. The package cannot be built without the bills and records.

grade.deliverable: PI lifecycle, in order, with the VA's task at each stage

match: All stages present and in order
Intake: documents collected, lead qualified
Claims set-up: claims opened, LOR sent, policy limits requested
Treatment: records and bills requested, lien tracking
Demand: package assembled
Negotiation and settlement: releases, net sheet, disbursement
nlp: Accept the short five-stage form as complete if each stage carries a VA task.
Order errors are scored separately from missing stages: a complete list in the wrong order caps at 60%.
An answer that lists stages with no VA task attached scores half — the question asks what the VA does.

trainer.feedback: Which stage they could not place…

v004.objective: Legal Intake: converting a contact into a client is the firm's most important process.
talk: This is where the case is won or lost before anyone looks at the law.
The information collected here is what every later stage runs on — Day 7 and Day 8 are entirely about it.
keys: Intake collects: client details, date of loss, how it happened, injuries, treatment so far, insurance on both sides, the police report.
pitfalls: Thinking intake is clerical. It is the firm's sales and evidence function at once.

v005.objective: The consultation: what the attorney covers with the client, and where the VA's limit is.
talk: The attorney discusses circumstances and concerns, and sets expectations.
The VA prepares, schedules and documents — the VA never advises on the merits or the value.
pitfalls: Answering a client's 'how much is my case worth'. That is the attorney's, always.

v006.objective: Investigation and how the firm gets paid: the contingency fee.
talk: Most PI lawyers work on contingency — a share of the settlement, nothing if the case loses, though costs may still apply.
Contrast with a retainer, which is paid up front. This exact comparison is a Day 7 Process Question.
keys: Contingency fee — a percentage of the recovery, charged only on a win; the client fronts no legal fee.
Retainer — paid up front and drawn down; typical of transactional and non-PI matters.
Effect on onboarding: contingency lowers the barrier to signing, so screening at intake does the filtering a fee would otherwise do.

v007.objective: Opening claims: contacting the insurer is one of the first steps, and it is the Claims Specialist's job.
talk: Insurers drive the pace of the whole case, especially in auto claims.
Days 10 to 12 are this one page in full: opening claims, LORs, and the SA workflow.

v008.objective: Claims set-up and liability: secure the documents, then identify every party at fault.
talk: Every possible at-fault party gets a claim opened with their insurer. Missing one loses coverage.
This is where UM/UIM gets opened — and failing to open it in time is a Day 10 Process Question.
keys: 1P = our client's own insurer. 3P = the at-fault party's insurer. Both get an LOR.
UM/UIM is opened against our client's own policy where the at-fault party has no or too little coverage. Late opening can forfeit the claim under the policy's notice terms.
pitfalls: Assuming one defendant means one claim. Multiple liable parties means multiple claims.

v009.objective: Policy limits and coverages: request the Dec Pages and read them.
talk: The firm requests the policy information for both plaintiff and defendant, then reads the declarations page.
The limit decides what the case can recover — this is the Day 11 Policy Disclosure activity.
keys: On a Dec Page, find: named insured, policy period, BI limits (per person / per accident), PD, UM/UIM, Med Pay or PIP, and any deductible.
A limit written 25/50/25 means $25,000 per person BI / $50,000 per accident BI / $25,000 PD.
pitfalls: Reading the per-accident figure as the per-person figure. It overstates the case by double or more.

v010.objective: Treatment begins: the client must treat promptly, and the records become the evidence.
talk: Treatment both heals the client and documents the injury — gaps in treatment are read as gaps in injury.
The Client Communication Specialist keeps that contact going.
pitfalls: Letting a client go quiet during treatment. A treatment gap is the single most common weakness in a claim.

v011.objective: What the client should keep while treating: providers seen, out-of-pocket costs, missed work.
talk: Those three feed the damages side of the demand. A VA who prompts for them early saves weeks later.

v012.objective: Collecting bills and records: when requests start, and why timing matters.
talk: Requests begin roughly 4–8 weeks after the date of loss, and in earnest as soon as treatment is complete.
Days 13 to 17 are this stage: MedLOR, bills and records, lien balance verification.
keys: Request sequence: MedLOR with the signed HIPAA authorization → bills and records → lien balance verification → the demand package.
pitfalls: Requesting records before the HIPAA authorization is valid and signed. The provider will refuse and the week is lost.

v013.objective: The firm coordinates with providers: all charges accounted for, treatment plan followed.
talk: Chasing a provider is normal work, not an exception — the Day 15 upskill covers assertive follow-ups.
Every charge must be accounted for before a demand goes out, or the demand understates the case.

v014.objective: The demand package: what it is and what it has to prove.
talk: It sets out the case, the injuries and the compensation sought, with the records behind it.
The goal is to make the adjuster's decision easy and well evidenced.
keys: A demand package carries: the demand letter, liability evidence (police report, photos), medical records and bills, wage loss proof, and the lien or LOP information.

v015.objective: What goes in the letter once everything is gathered.
talk: Medical bills, police report, evidence of fault — then the demand itself.
Each document in the package does a job: this is the Day 13 'Document Detectives' exercise.

v016.objective: The insurer reviews, then negotiation starts.
talk: The firm negotiates toward a satisfactory settlement; the first offer is rarely the last.
Packages can be submitted by mail, email or e-portal depending on the carrier.

v017.objective: Settlement: a voluntary agreement that ends the dispute.
talk: It speeds up resolution and removes the risk of trial for both sides.
Settlement is where the Lien Negotiator's work begins, not ends — Days 17 and 18.

v018.objective: Negotiations: the client is told immediately and the options are discussed.
talk: The firm notifies the client as soon as an offer arrives. Delay here is an ethics problem, not a scheduling one.
The options come from the attorney's experience; the VA documents and schedules.
pitfalls: A VA characterising an offer as good or bad to the client. Report it, do not evaluate it.

v019.objective: Disbursement: the settlement agreement, the deductions and what reaches the client.
talk: Reductions, liens, costs and fees come off before the client's net.
The net sheet and the closing statement must match to the cent — that is a Day 18 rule and a graded one.
keys: Order of operations: gross settlement → attorney's fee → case costs → medical liens and LOPs (after reduction) → net to client.
The net to client on the net sheet must equal the closing statement exactly.

v020.objective: Litigation: what happens when the insurer will not value the injuries properly.
talk: Most claims settle; a suit is filed when they do not.
Once suit is filed, deadlines become court deadlines — which is why calendaring is its own lesson.

v021.objective: Reception: the first point of contact, facing every kind of caller.
talk: Adjusters, opposing counsel, provider staff, courts and anxious clients all come through one line.
Tie it back to the tone matrix from Law Firm Communication, then forward to the Day 3–4 reception work.
keys: Reception's four jobs on every call: identify the caller, screen, triage, and document before transferring.

v022.objective: Calendar management: missed deadlines can dismiss a case or forfeit a right.
talk: Say the consequence out loud — dismissal, forfeiture. This is why Days 5 and 6 are strict.
Preview the rules they will be scored on: EST visible, 15-minute buffers, consult days and cut-offs.
keys: Standing calendar rules: everything in EST, 15-minute buffer before and after, email reminder one day prior, event titled [Meeting Type] – [Client Name].

v023.objective: Appointment Setter: keeps the client pipeline and the attorney's day working.
talk: Mandatory data on every setting call: name, callback number, DOB, DOL. No exceptions.
keys: Collect on every call: client name, callback number, Date of Birth, Date of Loss.

v024.objective: Scheduler: organized scheduling is what lets attorneys meet clients and hit tasks on time.
talk: Close the role list here, then move to the afternoon's work.

v025.objective: Close the deck, then run the afternoon: Process Questions, the confidentiality exercise, the call-listening set and the Call Intake & Data Extraction activity (six practice calls, five data points and the challenge each).
talk: Post the sample recordings, then set the Process Questions.
Run the Confidentiality & Call Response exercise after the questions.

Finish with Call Intake & Data Extraction on the Day 3 slides (the task in cards, then the six calls on one slide, whose Next is the Knowledge Check): six calls to Harbor & Pine Injury Law, each with a challenge (noise, a dropped line, a Spanish-speaking caller, an echo, a fast adjuster, a family member not on the file); five data points per call, and the challenge (the obstacle, the VA's response) — then give the CRM/CMS homework.

v001.objective: Open Receptionist Training: the firm's first impression is a job with rules, not a personality trait.
talk: Tell them the Day 4 mock calls are scored against six metrics, and name them now so they listen for each one.
Everything in this deck shows up in one of those six.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting Reception Training.

Your mock calls will be scored on six metrics:
• Greeting — 10%
• Intake Triage — 20%
• Tone & Empathy — 20%
• Confidentiality — 20%
• Data Accuracy — 15%
• Transfer & Notes — 15%

Listen for each of these as we go. Thank you.

keys: Reception Mock Call metrics: Greeting 10%, Intake Triage 20%, Tone/Empathy 20%, Confidentiality 20%, Data Accuracy 15%, Transfer/Notes 15%.

v038.objective: What to say when they do not know — never guess, never sound new.
talk: A receptionist who guesses creates a liability; one who says 'let me find out' creates confidence.
Have each trainee say one of the replacement phrases out loud. It has to be automatic by tomorrow.
keys: Use: 'Let me find out for you.' · 'I'd be happy to look into that.' · 'Great question — let me put you in touch with the best person to answer it.'
Never use: 'I don't know', 'I'm new here', 'I think…', or any answer about case value, liability or timing.
pitfalls: Filling a silence with a guess. That is the most common confidentiality failure in the mock calls.

v040.objective: Active listening, properly: paraphrase and read the message back word for word.
talk: Reading the message back catches the error while the caller is still on the line.
Make them practise it on each other now — it is 20% of tomorrow's Tone and Empathy mark and most of Data Accuracy.
keys: Read back: caller's name spelled out, callback number digit by digit, and the message in their words.
pitfalls: Paraphrasing the caller's emotion instead of their information.

v042.objective: Meticulous note-taking: spell names phonetically, confirm every number.
talk: Spell the name back using phonetics, then repeat the number in pairs.
Numbers are exact-match in grading — one wrong digit is a wrong field, not a near miss.
keys: Mandatory fields on a reception call: caller name (spelled), callback number, DOB, DOL, reason for the call, action taken.
pitfalls: Taking a name by sound alone. Spell it back, every time.

v044.objective: Authenticate before sharing anything — the hinge of the confidentiality metric.
talk: Gather the details and authenticate the caller before any information goes out, then transfer.
A caller who refuses to authenticate gets a message taken, not an answer.
keys: Authenticate on: full name, date of birth, and one case detail the caller should know. Only then does any case information move.
pitfalls: Confirming a detail the caller supplies. Confirming is disclosing.
Accepting 'I'm his wife' as authentication. It is not.

v047.objective: Adaptability: take initiative, think on their feet, stay calm under pressure.
talk: Close the best-practice run with the quality that cannot be scripted, then move to payment calls.
Initiative inside authority: act on the process, escalate the judgement.

v048.objective: Payment calls: who asks about money, and what a receptionist may say.
talk: Clients ask about balances; providers ask about treatment bills. Both are money calls and both are restricted.
Consultation fees and outstanding balances are figures from the system, never from memory.
keys: Quote only what the system shows, and only to an authenticated caller. Anything about a settlement figure goes to the attorney.

v049.objective: Authenticate, then double-check the figures in the system before saying any number.
talk: Accurate figures, clearly and confidently — but only after authentication.
If the system and the caller disagree, the system wins and the call is escalated.
pitfalls: Reading a figure off a stale note or an email instead of the system.

v050.objective: Walk the payment decision tree end to end — this is the escalation rule in diagram form.
talk: Enquiry → authenticate name and case ID → apply the compliance restriction → route or take a message.
Ask the room where the tree says stop. That point is the compliance restriction, and it is where most trainees keep talking.
keys: Handle independently: confirming an appointment, taking a message, giving the firm's own contact details, confirming a document was received.
Escalate: case value, liability, settlement timing, any figure not in the system, any caller who will not authenticate, any demand from opposing counsel or an adjuster.
pitfalls: Treating escalation as failure. Escalating correctly scores full marks on Intake Triage.

grade.deliverable: Payment-call decision tree — handle or escalate

match: Authenticates name and case ID before any figure
Applies the compliance restriction at the right branch
Routes to the right owner or takes a message
Does not state a settlement or case-value figure
nlp: Score the branch taken, not the wording: a correct escalation phrased awkwardly is still correct.
Any answer that discloses a figure before authentication fails the item outright.

scores.label: Handling of the caller at the stop point

rubric: Professional deference — escalates without apologising excessively
trainer.feedback: Where in the tree they went past the stop…

v051.objective: Cold transfers: what they are and why we do not use them.
talk: No warning, high risk of a dropped or disconnected call. Not recommended, and it costs marks on Transfer and Notes.

v052.objective: Warm transfers: the standard for this firm.
talk: Introduce both parties, or at least stay on until the call lands.
This is what Transfer and Notes is scored against tomorrow.
keys: Warm transfer script: tell the caller who they are going to and why, announce the caller and the reason to the recipient, then release.

v053.objective: Conference calls: a warm transfer where the receptionist stays on the line.
talk: Used when the caller needs both parties at once, or when a record of the exchange matters.

v054.objective: The closing reminder: tasks vary by client and by firm requirement.
talk: Back to SOP adherence from Lesson 1 — the firm's rule decides, not our habit.

v055.objective: Close the deck, set the Receptionist Process Questions and the confidentiality exercise, then move to mock call preparation.
talk: Set the Process Questions, then run the Confidentiality & Call Response exercise.
Spend what is left of the morning on mock call preparation: scripting, active listening, screening, the tone matrix.

keys: Answer anchors — first impression: verbal cues are tone, pace, clarity, the greeting itself and the read-back; non-verbal are the smile, posture and the pause before answering.

Answer anchor — misdirecting a caller: sending opposing counsel to the attorney unscreened, or a client to the wrong department, costs privilege and trust; both are confidentiality failures, not routing errors.

Answer anchor — screening before transfer: screen and note every call; escalate on value, liability, timing or an unauthenticated caller; handle appointments, messages and document confirmations independently.

match: Greeting names the firm and the VA, and offers help
Collects name, callback number, DOB and DOL

nlp: Score the transcript against the six metrics at their stated weights: Greeting 10, Intake Triage 20, Tone/Empathy 20, Confidentiality 20, Data Accuracy 15, Transfer/Notes 15.
Data Accuracy is exact-match on numbers (callback, DOB, DOL) and phonetic on names.
Any disclosure of case information to an unauthenticated caller, or any statement of case value or liability, zeroes the Confidentiality metric regardless of the rest.

Phone etiquette: no dead air, clean close

v002.objective: The first point of contact, and the range of callers who reach it.
talk: Name the caller types on the slide and say which of the six metrics each one tests.

v003.objective: Ready status from the moment the shift starts.
talk: Softphone open, CMS open, note template open — before the first ring, not after it.
pitfalls: Logging in at start of shift and then setting up for ten minutes.

v004.objective: Saving documents from fax and email, and tracking every call.
talk: The call log is the record. A call that is not logged did not happen as far as the file is concerned.

v005.objective: Common tasks: inquiry calls on existing clients, and sales calls.
talk: Two very different calls that both open the same way. The screen is what separates them.

v006.objective: Common tasks: opposing counsel, medical providers, court staff.
talk: Each of these three has its own rule, and all three are covered page by page ahead.

v007.objective: Common tasks: call routing, saving documents and fax.

v008.objective: What a lead is, and what a lead call needs.
talk: A lead is anyone who has expressed interest. Treat every one as the firm's next case.
keys: On a lead call: name, callback number, date of loss, what happened, whether they have counsel already.

v009.objective: Verify at surface level, then transfer to the right department.
talk: Surface verification, not an intake. Do not take the whole story and then transfer it second-hand.
pitfalls: Conducting a full intake at reception and leaving the specialist nothing to work with.

v010.objective: Existing client inquiries: the five things they usually want.
talk: Case updates, loans and payments, appointments, transportation, reaching the attorney.
Each has an owner. Reception's job is to route, not to answer.

v011.objective: When no case appears: the caller may be acting for the client.
talk: Parent, child, sibling, partner — plausible, and still not authorized until the file says so.
This is the setup for the authorization decision tree later in the deck.
pitfalls: Accepting a relationship as authority. Only the file decides.

v012.objective: Sales calls, and why they are a security matter.
talk: Unsolicited and often harmless, but the same opening is used to probe the firm.

v013.objective: Social engineering tactics — read each one aloud.
talk: Claiming prior meetings, pretending to know the attorneys, pressing for a name or a direct line.
The counter is boring and effective: take a message, confirm nothing.
keys: Never confirm who works there, who represents whom, or any direct line to an unverified caller. Take a message.
pitfalls: Correcting a caller who names the wrong attorney — the correction is the disclosure.

v014.objective: The ethics rule: lawyers do not communicate with represented opposing parties.
talk: This is a rule of professional conduct, and reception can breach it on the firm's behalf in one sentence.

v015.objective: Confirm with the attorney, case manager or paralegal before speaking to opposing counsel.
talk: Permission first, every time. Nobody is annoyed at being asked.

v016.objective: Confirm the caller is a licensed attorney, and never discuss case facts.
talk: Three rules on one page: verify, no facts, refer.
Have the room say the refusal sentence out loud so it exists before the mock call.
keys: Line to use: 'I'm not able to discuss the case — let me take your details and have the attorney call you back.'

v017.objective: Transfer or take a detailed message, then tag the attorney or paralegal.
talk: The tag is what makes the message land. An untagged note sits unread.

v018.objective: Medical provider calls: status, representation, claims, appointments.
talk: Representation can be confirmed. Treatment detail and case value cannot.
keys: Public information only to a provider: that we represent the client, the firm's contact details, where to send records.

v019.objective: Court staff calls on litigation cases.
talk: Formal, prepared, and routed to the litigation team.

v020.objective: Treat court calls as urgent: live or warm transfer, then the supervising attorney.
talk: Never a cold transfer and never voicemail without escalating. A court deadline may be on the line.
keys: If the attorney is unavailable: supervising attorney, then a detailed message with the case number, tagged immediately.

v021.objective: Insurance company calls: ALWAYS ask for the claim number and the DOL.
talk: Say it as the rule it is: no claim number and date of loss, no case located, nothing discussed.
keys: Collect from an adjuster: claim number, date of loss, carrier, adjuster's name and direct line. Then route.

v022.objective: What adjusters call about: demand responses, offers, liability decisions, IMEs, recorded statements.
talk: Every one of those is above reception's line. Route them, all of them.
pitfalls: Agreeing to a recorded statement, or confirming anything about a demand.

v023.objective: When they push: it is the firm's policy, and requests go in writing.
talk: Firm policy is a complete answer. Polite, repeatable, and no further explanation is owed.
This is the de-escalation the adjuster scenario is scored on tomorrow.
keys: Line to use: 'Any request will need to come in writing — that's the firm's policy. I'll note your call and have the handler follow up.'

v024.objective: Witnesses and the ethical rules on represented parties.
talk: Be cautious; do not interview. Take details and route.

v025.objective: The prohibition extends to any represented party, not only the adverse one.

v026.objective: Government and law enforcement calls: reports, FOIA requests, footage and 911 calls.
talk: These calls are routine but time-sensitive. Log and route the same day.
End them without engaging. Never press a key or confirm a name.

v028.objective: Mass tort and long-duration cases: Hernia Mesh, Zantac and their kind.
talk: Years long, little visible movement, so the caller is often frustrated before they say hello.

v029.objective: What to do on those calls: acknowledge the frustration, listen calmly.
talk: Acknowledge, do not defend. Never promise a timeline on a mass tort.
This is the de-escalation rubric in the mock calls, in its purest form.
keys: Acknowledge, confirm the file is active, say what the next step is if it is known, log the call, route to the handler. No timelines.
pitfalls: Explaining the delay. It reads as an excuse and invites an argument.

v030.objective: Authorization versus information: verify the authorized person, and who never gets information.
talk: This is the confidentiality metric in one page. Read the 'never release to' list aloud.
keys: Verify against the file's authorized-person list — not against how convincing the caller is.

v031.objective: Walk the authorization decision tree, branch by branch.
talk: Trace both paths out loud: listed in the CRM, and not listed.
Ask the room where the tree stops. That stop is where most trainees keep talking.
keys: Not listed as authorized: take a message, tell them the handler will contact the client, release nothing — not even whether the person is a client.
pitfalls: Confirming that someone is a client to an unauthorized caller. That alone is a disclosure.

v032.objective: Call routing: how calls reach their recipient.
talk: Sets up the cold, warm and conference transfer pages later in the deck.

v033.objective: Saving received documents and faxes to the right place.
talk: Same discipline as the SA document work from Day 8 onward: correct folder, correct name, reported.

v034.objective: The opening spiel: the firm's name and your name.
talk: Have every trainee say theirs now. It is 10% of tomorrow's mark and the easiest 10% to lose.
keys: Opening: 'Thank you for calling [firm], this is [name], how may I help you?'

v035.objective: Use the caller's name during the conversation.
talk: Twice is warm; every sentence is odd. Say that explicitly.

v036.objective: Sound enthusiastic and professional; stay composed whatever the caller says.
talk: Mind tone and volume, let the caller speak first, and do not take the content personally.
Composure is what the hostile-caller scenario is scored on.

v037.objective: Smiling is the shortcut to the right tone.
talk: It sounds like a cliché and it measurably works. Say it once and move on.

v039.objective: The phrases to use instead — practise them aloud.
talk: Each trainee says one. They need to arrive without thinking tomorrow.

v041.objective: Repeating the message back also catches the mistake while the caller is still there.
talk: Reassurance and quality control in the same move.

v043.objective: Attentiveness: review the notes during the call, use context to get past difficulty.
talk: For an existing client, reading the file while they talk is what makes the call short and useful.
pitfalls: Asking an existing client questions the file already answers.

v045.objective: Adjusting to the situation: manage time, note, email and notify at once.
talk: Multitasking here means the note is written during the call, not after it.

v046.objective: Stay calm under pressure and prioritize.
talk: Close the adaptability thread, then move to payment calls.

v001.objective: Open Calendar Management: a missed date can dismiss a case, so this lesson is scored on rules, not habits.
talk: Say the stakes first — dismissal, forfeiture of rights.
Tell them the firm's own rules override every general tip in this deck, and that the rules are what the activity and the mock calls are scored against.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting Appointment Setting and Calendar Management.

As we go, write down the FIRM'S rules — they override the general tips in the deck and they are what your activity and mock calls are scored on:
• The calendar is in EST, and the time zone must be VISIBLE in every screenshot.
• Event title format: [Meeting Type] – [Client Name]
• Collect on every call: Name, Callback Number, DOB, DOL.
• 15-minute buffer before and after every meeting.
• Email reminder one day prior.

Thank you.

keys: Firm rules to repeat at every opportunity today: EST and visible, [Meeting Type] – [Client Name], Name/Callback/DOB/DOL, 15-minute buffers, email reminder one day prior.

v002.objective: Set the objective: a structured approach to managing someone else's time, not their own.
talk: The calendar they manage belongs to an attorney. Every decision is made on the attorney's behalf and to the attorney's rules.

v003.objective: The agenda, one line each: basics, organization and setup, scheduling best practices, interruptions and flexibility.
talk: Flag that the firm rules sit inside 'scheduling best practices' — that is the part that is graded.

v004.objective: Why it matters: organization, deadlines, and the balance of commitments.
talk: Keep it short. The general case for calendars is not what they are tested on.

v005.objective: Time management and avoiding overlaps — double-booking is the failure mode.
talk: Prevent double-booking and over-scheduling. In a law firm an overlap means the attorney misses one of them.
This is why the 15-minute buffer exists: back-to-back meetings become overlaps the moment one runs long.
keys: A double-booking in the activity or the mock calls is an automatic deduction, not a style point.

v006.objective: The calendars we use: Google Calendar and Outlook.
talk: Google Calendar is what the activity and the mock calls are performed in.
Outlook appears at firms that run Microsoft — the rules do not change with the platform.

v007.objective: Shared calendars, and single versus multiple.
talk: An attorney's calendar is shared. Anything plotted is visible to the firm immediately, so a wrong entry is seen before it is fixed.
keys: For the activity screenshots: untick the LSH calendar before capturing the full-calendar view, then re-enable it.

v008.objective: Time zones, event creation and colour coding — and the firm's EST rule.
talk: Teach the time-zone setting properly: this is where most activity marks are lost.
Set the appropriate time zone for each item, and take the screenshot BEFORE saving so the time zone is captured.
keys: The calendar runs in EST. The time zone must be visible in the screenshot of every individual appointment.
No separate screenshot of the time zone is needed — it just has to be visible in each appointment's own capture.
pitfalls: Plotting in local time and converting afterwards.
Saving the appointment first and then trying to screenshot the time zone.

v009.objective: Open the setup section: a calendar set up properly is what stops missed deadlines.

v010.objective: Steps 1–2: define the categories, set up the calendar.
talk: Categories for a PI firm: consultations, follow-ups, case meetings, signings, court dates, deadlines.

v011.objective: Steps 3–4: recurring events, then deadlines and events.
talk: Deadlines are not meetings. Plot them as their own entries with reminders, not as appointments.

v012.objective: Steps 5–6: time blocking, then the weekly and monthly review.
talk: Time blocking is optional; the weekly review is not. Encourage a Monday-morning pass over the attorney's week.

v013.objective: Step 7–8: reminders and flexibility — and the firm's reminder rule.
talk: Reminders are the deliverable, not a nicety: the attorney has to be reminded, by email, a day before.
Flexibility means the buffer absorbs the overrun, not that the rules bend.
keys: Set an EMAIL reminder one day prior on every event plotted. This is checked in the activity and in the mock calls.
pitfalls: Leaving the default notification (10 minutes, pop-up) in place. It is not the firm's rule.

v014.objective: Managing reminders: do not overload; prioritize and categorize.
talk: Too many reminders and the attorney stops reading them — which is the same as having none.
Note them and move on; the firm's reminder lives on the calendar event itself.

v016.objective: Keeping the client's calendar current: consistency and colour coding.
talk: Review and update regularly. A calendar is only trusted if it is current.

v017.objective: Weekly reviews and buffer times — where the 15-minute rule lands.
talk: Introduce the buffer properly here, then make it concrete with the firm's number.
Ask the room what happens to the 2:00 appointment when the 1:30 runs ten minutes over without a buffer.
keys: The attorney requires a 15-minute buffer BEFORE and AFTER every meeting. Not 10. Not 'some'.
pitfalls: Buffering only after a meeting. The rule is both sides.

talk: Keep it brief — the firm's platform is already chosen.

v019.objective: Colour-coding categories, and how to create a colour label.
talk: Useful, but never a substitute for a clear title. The title is what is graded.

v020.objective: Labels and descriptions — the firm's event naming rule and the note content.
talk: Clear descriptions avoid ambiguity. Our format is not optional.
Walk one example end to end: title, notes with case context, and the caller's demeanour recorded in the notes.
keys: Event title: [Meeting Type] – [Client Name]. For example 'Client Consultation Meeting – Jane Smith'.
The notes carry the case context and the instruction from the caller, e.g. 'New PI case; client requests afternoon callback'.
pitfalls: Titles like 'Consultation' or 'Call' with no client name. It fails the activity item outright.

v021.objective: Categorizing by priority with the action priority matrix.
talk: High priority in a PI firm means anything with a legal deadline attached.

v023.objective: The Eisenhower matrix, applied to an attorney's week.
talk: Urgent and important: court deadlines, statute dates. Important not urgent: case strategy. Urgent not important: most inbound calls.
A VA's judgement call is which inbound requests get same-day slots — and our rule is that same-day bookings need attorney approval.
keys: Same-day bookings require attorney approval. No exceptions in the mock calls.

v024.objective: Scheduling meetings: do not over-schedule, leave transition time.
talk: The deck says 10–15 minutes. Our firm says 15, before and after. Our number wins.
This is the page to state the durations the firm uses, because the mock calls are scored on them.
keys: Durations: 30 minutes — consultations, status updates, follow-ups, signings, regular and urgent meetings. 45 minutes — preparation, strategy and settlement meetings. 1 hour — conference meetings.
New client consults: Tuesdays and Thursdays only, maximum 3 per day, none after 5:00 PM EST.
All consultation meetings are phone consults, between 9:30 AM and 3:00 PM EST; the attorney calls the client, so the callback number must be confirmed.
Follow-ups are never scheduled in the morning.
pitfalls: Offering a new client consult on a Monday or Wednesday.
Booking a 30-minute slot for a strategy meeting, which needs 45.

v025.objective: Managing interruptions: flexible time for overruns and urgent tasks.
talk: The buffer is the flexibility. Nothing else gets moved without the attorney's say.

v026.objective: Buffer time, defined properly: deliberate space to absorb delay.
talk: Close the buffer thread here — they should be able to state the 15-minute rule without prompting.

v028.objective: Recurring events and the frequency options.
talk: Physical therapy courses are the common recurring series in a PI file.

v030.objective: The Pomodoro technique, in one line.
talk: Personal productivity, not a firm rule. Keep it moving.

v031.objective: Why time pressure makes people work worse, not faster.

v032.objective: How Pomodoro works, and blocking it on a calendar.

talk: Useful for VA inbox work: anything under two minutes is done now, not calendared.

v034.objective: The 80/20 rule applied to the attorney's tasks.
talk: The 20% in a PI firm is anything that moves a case toward demand or settlement.

v035.objective: Last-minute changes: stay flexible, use notifications.
talk: Script it: when the attorney moves a meeting, the VA re-plots it, re-sets the reminder, and tells the client — in that order.

v036.objective: Work-life balance and boundaries on the client's calendar.

v037.objective: Preventing over-scheduling: realistic durations, white space.
talk: Tie back to the firm's durations and the 3-consults-a-day cap.
Avoid lunch, buffer time and blocked events when offering slots — that is a scored behaviour in the mock calls.
keys: When a requested slot is unavailable, offer 2–3 alternatives. Never offer a slot that sits on lunch, a buffer or a blocked event.

v041.objective: The schedule as work in progress.

v042.objective: Owning the executive's time, and reviewing it regularly.

talk: Then move straight to the activity — the morning's marks are there, not here.
Use this page to set up the Day 6 mock calls: the scorecard below is what each call is marked against.

match: Collected all four: name, callback number, DOB, DOL
Clarified the meeting type (phone, video, in-person)
Offered only available slots; 2-3 alternatives where the request was taken
Event plotted in EST with the title [Meeting Type] - [Client Name]
Correct duration for the meeting type (30 / 45 / 60 minutes)
15-minute buffer before and after
Email reminder set one day prior
Notes carry the case context and the caller's demeanour
nlp: Score the plotted event against the rules as structured fields, and the call itself against the collection and offer rules.

A slot that breaks a hard rule - a new client consult outside Tuesday/Thursday, after 5:00 PM EST, a fourth consult in a day, a phone consult outside 9:30 AM-3:00 PM, a morning follow-up, or a same-day booking without attorney approval - fails the scheduling item however well the call was handled.
Accept any phrasing for confirming the callback number; it is the confirmation that is scored, not the words.

scores.label: Calendar entry: title, duration, buffer, reminder

rubric: Call tone adapted to the caller (easy, anxious, irritated, impatient, emotional)
Professional deference on an urgent attorney request
Phone etiquette: clean open and close
trainer.feedback: Which scheduling rule they broke, and how they handled being told the slot was unavailable...

v044.objective: Close the deck and run the Attorney Calendar Management activity, then set up the Day 6 mock calls.
talk: Post the activity and the sample screenshots together — the samples are what the sequence and the time-zone capture are judged against.
Walk the screenshot rules before they start, or half the batch will re-do them: time zone visible, correct numbering, 19 screenshots, LSH calendar unticked for the full-calendar view.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting Intake Specialist Training.

This deck carries you through Days 7, 8 and 9: today's discussion and breakout, then the intake documents, then your Smart Advocate demo and your intake mock calls.

Please take notes as we go — the intake packet documents and the fee arrangements are both graded later. Thank you.

v002.objective: The table of contents: intake specialist, consultation, scheduling.

v003.objective: Converting contacts into clients is the firm's most important process.
talk: Same line as the PI Workflow deck — repeat it deliberately. It is the one claim in this program worth repeating.

v004.objective: The goal is quality, not quantity: schedule GOOD leads for consultation.
talk: A bad lead booked costs a consultation slot the attorney cannot get back.
Ask the room what makes a lead good before you answer: injury, treatment, liability, insurance, and within the statute.
keys: A good lead has: an injury, treatment either started or intended, a liable party, insurance to claim against, and a date of loss inside the statute.

v005.objective: The information collected opens the case — which is why intake digs deep.
talk: Everything they collect is used by somebody else later. Thin intake is re-work for four other roles.

v006.objective: Intake shapes the consultation; the end goal is the appointment.
talk: Close the introduction, then move into what a good intake system needs.

v007.objective: Requirement 1: capture contact information, and know where leads come from.
talk: Referral, walk-in, web, ad — the source changes the tone, never the questions.
keys: Capture name and callback number FIRST, before the story. Calls drop.

v008.objective: Requirements 2 and 3: pre-screening and conflict checking, before a consultation is booked.
talk: Pre-screening saves the attorney's time; the conflict check protects the firm's ability to take the case at all.
Flag that conflicts get a whole section of this deck — they are not a formality.
pitfalls: Booking the consultation first and checking for conflicts afterwards.

v009.objective: Requirements 4 and 5: holding the consultation, and collecting key information.

v010.objective: Requirements 6 and 7: the fee agreement signed, then onboarding.
talk: The signed agreement is the first document of the intake packet, and the one everything else depends on.

v011.objective: Walk the lead call flow chart out loud — this is the call they will perform on Day 9.
talk: Trace one path end to end: greeting, contact details, screening questions, conflict questions, commitment, appointment.
Then trace the path where the lead is NOT good, so they know how that call ends politely.
keys: Every path ends with a commitment or a clear next step — never 'we'll see'.

v012.objective: Required information: what the attorney will use it for.
talk: The attorney evaluates needs, determines viability and decides whether to take the case. Thin answers mean a wrong decision.

v013.objective: Insurance policy, and the names and contacts of everyone involved.
talk: Car or homeowner's policy, every person involved, and how to reach them.
Names of all drivers, passengers and employers are also what surfaces a conflict later.

v014.objective: Accident description — get their account early, because accounts change.
talk: Record it in their words, early. A later version that contradicts the first is damaging.
pitfalls: Summarising instead of recording. Write what they said.

v015.objective: Injuries and the client's own insurance — ask early.
talk: Aches and pains reported days later are harder to attribute. Ask on the first call.
Their own insurance matters for UM/UIM and Med Pay, which the Claims Specialist will need.

v016.objective: Defendant information and the emergency contact.
talk: Whatever they can get on the defendant. An emergency contact also keeps a quiet client reachable.

v017.objective: Witness accounts are most useful when contacted early.
talk: Get names and numbers on the first call; witnesses become unreachable fast.

v018.objective: The document checklist — read it against what intake actually receives.
talk: Tell them a packet is often incomplete, and that the SOP is to save what came and flag what did not.
This is exactly the Day 8 and Day 9 activity.
keys: Missing documents: extract, rename and save only what is present, follow SOP for the gap, and notify the Case Manager or Attorney. Never contact the client directly unless authorized.
