talk: Photographs of injuries and a sketch of how it happened. Both age badly — ask on the first call.

v032.objective: Police exchange sheets, specialist reports, reconstruction reports.

v033.objective: The police or incident report — the official account.
talk: This is the document that most often decides whether liability is contested.
It is also where the information we may share with an adjuster comes from.

v034.objective: Medical records — and the signature we need to request them.
talk: No signed authorization, no records. This is the HIPAA form, and it comes back on Day 13 and Day 14.

v035.objective: Insurance policies: we read them to find every coverage that may apply.
talk: Ties straight to the Day 11 Dec Page activity.

v036.objective: Incident statement: the client's written account, before, during and after.

v037.objective: Witness statements, recorded as soon as possible.

v038.objective: Video of the incident: canvass for traffic and security cameras.
talk: Footage is overwritten in days. This is the most time-critical item on the list.

v039.objective: Bills and insurance papers — the client keeps everything.

v040.objective: Employment records and tax forms, for lost income.

v041.objective: Specialists retained to review evidence and testify.

v042.objective: The daily journal: the client's own record of the experience.
talk: Prompt it at intake. Nobody can reconstruct it later.

v043.objective: Open conflicts properly: they arise before a case is accepted, some are non-waivable, and intake does NOT decide.
talk: Say the third line twice: Intake Specialists do not decide conflicts. They surface them and escalate.
Tell them the nine conflict types that follow are not trivia — missing one can cost the firm the case and more.
keys: Intake's job on a conflict: ask the questions, record every name, flag it, escalate to the attorney. Never reassure the caller that it is fine.
pitfalls: A trainee deciding a conflict is 'probably nothing' and booking the consult anyway.

v044.objective: Existing or prior representation — the most critical, usually non-waivable.
talk: Defendant driver, at-fault business, property owner. Any of these already with the firm and the call stops.

v045.objective: Two drivers from the same collision: the firm cannot represent both.

v046.objective: Multiple claimants from one incident — waivable or not, depending on jurisdiction and the facts.
talk: Limited policy limits are what turns multiple claimants into a real conflict.

v047.objective: Insurance carrier conflicts — often missed at intake.
talk: Ask which carrier, every time, on both sides.

v048.objective: Former client conflicts, triggered even on an unrelated matter.

v049.objective: Employer–employee conflicts, common on work-injury calls.
talk: Always capture the employer's name. This is the question trainees forget.

v050.objective: Government and public entity conflicts, with strict disclosure requirements.
talk: A city, county or state defendant also brings short notice deadlines. Escalate the same day.

v051.objective: Medical provider and lien conflicts, which can affect settlement integrity.

v052.objective: Personal conflicts of attorneys or staff — still flagged at intake.
talk: It is not awkward to ask; it is the job.

v053.objective: Prior consultation conflicts, even where no representation followed.
talk: Information shared in a consultation is protected. A prior consult with the other side is a conflict.

v054.objective: The intake red flags VAs must capture on every call — the practical version of the whole section.
talk: Make them write this list down and read it back. It is the one page from the conflicts section they must carry into a live call.
keys: Capture on every intake call: names of all drivers, passengers and employers; the insurance companies on both sides; the defendant and any business or property owner; whether the caller has spoken to or been represented by another firm; any prior consultation with our firm.
pitfalls: Capturing only the caller's own details. The conflict usually hides in the other names.

grade.deliverable: Conflict red flags — surfaced and escalated correctly

match: All driver, passenger and employer names captured
Carriers on both sides captured
Defendant / business / property owner identified
Prior or current representation asked about
Prior consultation with our firm asked about
Flagged and escalated rather than resolved by the trainee
nlp: Score capture and escalation separately: capturing a conflict and then reassuring the caller scores zero on escalation.
Any answer in which the trainee decides a conflict is waivable is a hard fail — that decision is the attorney's.

rubric: Asked the uncomfortable questions without hedging
Professional deference — escalated rather than ruled
Kept the caller comfortable while asking
trainer.feedback: Which red flag they let pass…

v055.objective: The training note for Legal VAs — read it aloud, in full.
talk: This page is the boundary of the role. Do not paraphrase it.

v057.objective: Name and contact details first, accurately, at the start of the call.
talk: Spell the name back, repeat the number in pairs. Same rule as reception.

v058.objective: Active listening in a mostly one-sided conversation.
talk: The lead talks; the VA stays engaged and steers. Silence is not listening.

v059.objective: Ask permission and set expectations about the caller's time.

v060.objective: Ask specific questions — be direct about what identifies the case.
talk: Open questions get a story; specific questions get a case. Both are needed, in that order.

v061.objective: Get a commitment — never end on an open or uncertain note.
talk: This is the difference between a lead and a scheduled consultation.

v062.objective: The commitment script, word for word.
talk: Have each trainee say it once now, so it is ready for the Day 9 mock calls.
keys: Script: 'Your information will be reviewed by our office and we will follow up with you within today.' Then state when, and who will call.

v063.objective: Assess the impact: review intake regularly to improve it.

v064.objective: Open the intake packet section — the documents they will extract, rename and save on Days 8 and 9.
talk: Tell them now: every document on the coming pages has a naming convention, and the name is graded.

v065.objective: What the intake packet is, and who sends it.
talk: All the intake documents the firm uses to open a case. The Intake Specialist assembles and sends it.

v066.objective: Agreement for Representation: the contract that hires the firm.
talk: Fee terms, scope, and what the client is agreeing to. This is the document the whole packet turns on.

v067.objective: Agreement for Representation: exclusivity — no settling or negotiating without the attorney.
talk: Worth saying to the room: this is why a VA never discusses an offer with a client.

v068.objective: Sample Agreement for Representation — walk the signature and date blocks.
talk: Point at where the client's signature and date go, because an unsigned agreement is the most common packet defect.

v070.objective: Statement of Client's Rights, sample — point at the fields only.

v071.objective: HIPAA Authorization: what it permits and what makes it valid.
talk: This is the single most consequential form in the packet for the Provider Communication role.
keys: Filling the HIPAA form: the Validity of Authorization date is the date the CLIENT SIGNED, as shown below the document. Relationship to Patient is 'Self'.
An expired or misdated authorization gets the records request refused.

v072.objective: HIPAA Authorization, sample — show the signature date and the validity field.

v073.objective: HITECH: access to records under the Act.

v074.objective: Request for Complete Medical Records, including imaging.

v076.objective: Affidavit of Consent to Release Police Report Information.

talk: Medicare and Medicaid come back on Day 17 as government health plans with their own reduction rules.

v080.objective: Notice of Termination of Representation — used when a client leaves a previous firm.
talk: Its presence in a packet is also a conflict signal. Flag it.

v082.objective: Joint Acceptance of Common Legal Representation, after full disclosure.
talk: This is the document behind the multiple-claimant conflict from earlier.

v083.objective: Joint Acceptance, continued — advantages, risks and waiver.

v085.objective: Waiver of Conflict of Interest: the rules it sets out.

v086.objective: Adverse interests — no representing directly conflicting clients.

v087.objective: Business transactions with clients, generally prohibited.

v089.objective: Conflict of Interest form, sample, page 1.

v090.objective: Conflict of Interest form, sample, page 2.
talk: Note the latest version is the Notice and Waiver of Potential Conflict of Interest — the Day 8 reference set has it.

v091.objective: Client Information Sheet: the details the case documentation runs on.

v093.objective: ISO Claim Search Disclosure Request: the client's insurance claim history.
talk: Prior claims change how an adjuster values this one. Expect it in the packet.

v095.objective: 3rd Party Insurance Affidavit and its key sections.
talk: This is the affidavit that rides with a 3P LOR on Day 12.

v097.objective: Retainer fees: an advance payment to secure the attorney's services.
talk: Set up the comparison properly — retainer against contingency is a graded Process Question.
keys: Retainer — paid up front, drawn down against work performed. Common outside PI.

v098.objective: Billable hours: the work attorneys bill to clients.

v099.objective: What is NOT billable: administration, management, training, general email.
talk: Useful for them: it is why clear, specific time entries matter.

v100.objective: Contingency fees — and the costs the client may still owe.
talk: Nothing charged unless the case wins, but filing fees, experts and discovery costs can still fall to the client.
Now run the comparison out loud: how does each arrangement change onboarding and expectations?
keys: Contingency — a percentage of the recovery, charged only on a win; case costs may still be the client's.
Effect on onboarding: contingency removes the up-front barrier, so screening at intake does the filtering; expectations must be set about costs and about timelines.
pitfalls: Telling a client 'it costs you nothing'. Case costs are not the fee.

grade.deliverable: Process Questions — Intake Specialist Training (Priority track, 5 questions)

match: Supporting documents tied to BOTH liability and damages
Third-party collection: named hurdles (authorization, fees, backlog, portals) AND a stated workaround
Intake packet components each given a purpose
Case-type customization: a named example where a generic packet fails
Retainer vs contingency both defined, with the effect on onboarding
nlp: Score per question against the answer anchors; five questions, equal weight.
On documents, require the split: an answer that only says 'they prove the case' scores half.
On fees, an answer that says contingency costs the client nothing at all is marked wrong on that item — case costs remain.

trainer.feedback: Which of the five to revisit before the Day 9 mock calls…

v102.objective: Consultation scheduling once intake is complete — always against the attorney's calendar.
talk: Back to the Lesson 5 rules: available slots only, no double-booking, confirm the callback number.
keys: Consults are phone consults between 9:30 AM and 3:00 PM EST, Tuesdays and Thursdays for new clients, max 3 a day, none after 5:00 PM.

v103.objective: Calls that need scheduling immediately, or endorsing.
talk: Same-day needs attorney approval. Urgency does not override the rule; it escalates it.

v104.objective: Remember! — close on the reminder page.
talk: Then set the breakout and the shadowing.

v105.objective: Close the deck, run the breakout, post the reference set, and set up the afternoon's shadowing.
talk: Post the three handouts, run the five Priority questions, then the Intake Scenario Exercise.
Post the reference broadcast: insurance providers, the evidence checklist, the fillable forms, the mock intake audio.
Confirm the shadowing slot with the shadow buddy, give the trainees their times, and correct the TAM wording before they log it.

v001.objective: Open the Claims Specialist role: Days 10, 11 and 12 all run from this deck.
talk: Today is the discussion and the breakout; tomorrow is the Dec Page activity and LOR drafting; Day 12 is the SA demo.
Tell them the guardrails on what may be said to an adjuster come up early and are non-negotiable.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting Insurance Communication — the Claims Specialist Role.

This deck carries Days 10 to 12: today's discussion and breakout, tomorrow's Policy Disclosure and Claim & Liability Evaluation plus your LOR drafting, and then your recorded demo for uploading and sending LORs in Smart Advocate.

Please take notes — the Dec Page reading and the LOR formatting rules are both graded. Thank you.

v006.objective: Coverage information from the police report — and the data guardrails that go with it.
talk: The police report is where the carrier names and policy information usually come from.
This is the page to put the guardrails on the board, because it is where they realise the adjuster already has most of it.
keys: DO NOT SHARE with an adjuster: Date of Birth, Email address, SSN, VIN.
MAY SHARE: client's first and last name only (no middle name), vehicle information such as the plate number, city and state only, and the law firm's phone number.
Why those are safe: they are already in the police report the adjuster holds.
pitfalls: Giving the client's own number instead of the firm's.
Confirming a DOB the adjuster reads out — confirming is disclosing.

v012.objective: Close the opening-a-claim sequence: what has to be true before the call ends.
talk: Run the checklist out loud; this is the page with no written script, so the cue is the script.
Then move into claim filing.
keys: Before ending an opening call: claim number, adjuster's name spelled back, adjuster's direct number and extension, email or fax for documents, and the carrier's preferred method of receipt.
pitfalls: Ending the call without the adjuster's direct line. Every later task needs it.

v013.objective: PIP and UM/UIM: what the attorney will direct them to open, and the deadline risk.
talk: Attorneys will usually direct PIP and/or UM claims. Opening them late is the risk.
This is Process Question 2, and the most consequential one on the sheet.
keys: UM/UIM is opened under our client's own policy where the at-fault party has no coverage or not enough.
Late notice can forfeit the claim under the policy's own notice terms, and the firm — not the carrier — carries that failure.
pitfalls: Waiting for the 3P carrier to deny before opening UM/UIM.

v016.objective: Confirm and double-check: claim number, adjuster's name spelling, direct line.
talk: Spell the adjuster's name back. It goes into SA and onto every letter after this.
keys: Record in SA: policy number, claim number, the carrier's actual name, the adjuster's full name and contact. Where no adjuster is assigned yet, write 'No adjuster assigned yet.' and still enter everything else.

v024.objective: LOR recipients: 1P, 3P, opposing counsel — everyone who must be told.
talk: Day 12's demo sends both. Name them now: 1P to our client's carrier, 3P with the affidavit to the at-fault carrier.
keys: Naming convention for Day 12: INS – 1P/3P Insurance Provider - LOR mm.dd.yy (VA's name).
For example: INS – 1P State Farm – LOR 02.17.2026 (Michelle) · INS – 3P Geico – LOR with Affidavit 02.17.2026 (Michelle).

v028.objective: LOR drafting: what has to be in the letter, and the formatting rules that are graded.
talk: Adjuster's name in the letter, the notice to the carrier, the time frame, the policy copy request and the preservation request.
Then give the formatting rules for tomorrow's drafting activity — these are where marks are actually lost.
keys: 'F/E' means Fax or Email. Pick ONE based on the case notes.
In the recipient's address block, keep only the method chosen and delete the other from 'SENT VIA FACSIMILE AND E-MAIL'.
Replace the 'F/E' placeholder with the actual fax number or email address being used.
NO HIGHLIGHTED TEXT may remain in the final output. Check formatting: spacing, address block layout, consistent font and alignment.
pitfalls: Leaving both send methods in the header.
Leaving highlighted placeholder text in a letter that goes to an insurance company.
Drafting from the template without reading the case notes for the send method.

grade.file: Both letters saved in Assessments/Activities, per the activity sheet

match: Send method matches the case notes (fax or email), one only
'SENT VIA FACSIMILE AND E-MAIL' reduced to the chosen method
'F/E' replaced with the actual fax number or email address
No highlighted text remains
Adjuster name, claim number and policy number match the case notes exactly
Policy copy request and evidence preservation request both present
nlp: Compare every name, number and date against the case notes field by field; a mismatch is wrong, not partial.
Detect remaining highlight runs in the document body — any remaining highlight fails the formatting item.
Score content and formatting separately: these letters go to insurers, so a correct letter that still carries a placeholder is not a pass.

rubric: Asked about an ambiguous case note rather than guessing
trainer.feedback: What would have had to be fixed before this letter could be sent…

v031.objective: Sending the LOR by the entity's preferred method — and the MetroFax format.
talk: Preferred method comes from the case notes or the adjuster. Then show the fax conversion, because the demo is marked on it.
keys: MetroFax: remove the dashes, add +1 at the front, append @metrofax.com. 702-998-2171 becomes +17029982171@metrofax.com.
Subject line: Client Name - Insurance Company - Letter of Representation.
Faxed and e-filed letters carry a manual signature block: full name, Insurance Claims Specialist, work email, firm phone.
TIP: fill the recipient box LAST, so an unfinished letter cannot be sent.
Return 5–10 minutes after sending to check for the successful transmission message; resend until it confirms.
pitfalls: Leaving the dashes in the fax number.
Filling the recipient first and sending a half-finished letter.

v036.objective: The Declarations Page: the certified copy of the policy, and what it tells us.
talk: Call it both names — Dec Page and certified copy of policy — because both appear in case notes.
Tomorrow's activity is read entirely off these pages.

v040.objective: Verify every listed item on the Dec Page — the page with no script, and the one the activity is built on.
talk: Walk the review list field by field: policyholder, policy period, insured vehicles, coverages, limits, deductibles, endorsements.
Have them say what each field changes about the claim.
keys: Check on every Dec Page: named insured and whether our client is covered under it, policy period against the date of loss, insured vehicles, each coverage and its limit, deductibles, and endorsements.
A date of loss outside the policy period is the single most important thing to catch — the policy does not respond at all.
pitfalls: Reading the limits without checking the policy period against the DOL.
Reading the per-accident figure as the per-person figure.

v043.objective: Bodily Injury Liability — what it pays and who it protects.
talk: BI is the coverage the whole 3P claim runs on. Everything in the demand is aimed at it.

v045.objective: UM and UIM coverage, properly distinguished.
talk: UM for no coverage at all, UIM for not enough. They are different claims and both are opened under our client's policy.
keys: UM — the at-fault party has no insurance. UIM — the at-fault party has insurance, but less than the damages.
Both come off our client's own policy, which is why the Dec Page for the 1P side matters as much as the 3P.

v048.objective: Split limits: per person and per accident.
talk: This is the structure they will see most often. Make them read one aloud.
25/50/25 means $25,000 per person BI, $50,000 per accident BI, $25,000 PD.
keys: Per person caps what ONE claimant can recover; per accident caps what EVERYONE recovers together.
pitfalls: Telling a client the per-accident figure is what their claim is worth.

talk: One pot for all bodily injury and property damage in the accident. Less common in personal auto, standard in commercial.

v051.objective: Aggregate limits: the maximum across the policy period.

v052.objective: Umbrella policies: extra liability that starts where the underlying limits end.
talk: Always ask whether one exists. It is often the difference between a limited and a full recovery.

v062.objective: Partial liability: more than one party shares responsibility.
talk: Set up comparative liability here, then do the arithmetic on the example page.
keys: Comparative liability reduces the recovery by the client's share of fault.

v066.objective: The comparative liability arithmetic — do it on the board.
talk: $100,000 in damages with the client 25% at fault recovers $75,000. Have them compute a second one.
This is Process Question 3; the answer is the arithmetic plus what it does to strategy.
keys: Damages × (1 − client's share of fault) = recoverable amount. $100,000 at 25% fault = $75,000.
Strategy effect: the carrier argues the client's percentage up, so the liability evidence from intake is what holds it down.

match: Correct arithmetic on the worked example
Names the client's fault share as the reducing factor
States who argues the percentage and what rebuts it
nlp: The number is exact-match; the reasoning is scored semantically.
An answer that says partial fault bars recovery entirely is wrong — flag it for re-teaching, it is a common misconception.

rubric: Worked it without a calculator prompt
Connected it back to the intake evidence
trainer.feedback: Whether the gap was the maths or the concept…

v063.objective: Liability versus coverage — the distinction trainees miss.
talk: Admitting liability is not the same as agreeing to pay. Coverage can still be denied.

v064.objective: Liability accepted, coverage denied: what to do next.
talk: This is where UM/UIM becomes the route. Escalate to the attorney the same day.

v067.objective: Liability denial: what it means for the file.

v074.objective: The liability and coverage guide — the summary table.
talk: Use this page as the recap before the breakout. Have them read each row's consequence.

v076.objective: Role flexibility by client requirement — back to SOP adherence.
talk: Same point as Lesson 1, in a claims context: the client firm's process wins.

v077.time: 2 hrs (breakout, until ~3:00 PM) + PM video review
v077.objective: Close the deck, run the breakout, then set the afternoon's video and SOP review.
talk: Post the three handouts, run the seven Priority questions, then the Claims Terminology Exercise.
Post the adjuster guardrails again in writing — they are the thing most likely to be got wrong in a live call.
Then set the afternoon: the opening-claims and LOR videos, the Zurich demo, and the VLF 3P SOP.

gc.label: Process Questions — Priority track (7)
gc.text:
PROCESS QUESTIONS

1. Evaluate the consequences of failing to open a UM/UIM claim in time. What are the procedural and legal risks?
2. Assess the impact of a delayed or poorly written LOR on the efficiency of a claim's progress.
3. Break down a case scenario: the claimant was partially at fault. How does comparative liability affect coverage decisions?
4. Analyze how personal auto insurance and rideshare company insurance interact in accident claims involving Uber or Lyft.
5. Assess the advantages and limitations of pursuing a claim through a rideshare company's insurance vs. the driver's personal policy.
6. Judge how much automation (e.g. calendar reminders, templates) is appropriate in the claim process without losing the personal touch.
7. Evaluate the ethical and legal responsibilities of notifying the client when a case is dropped.

Save your answers in your Assessments/Activities folder as:

keys: Full list is 10 questions; the Priority track is the 7 above.

Answer anchor — rideshare: the driver's personal policy usually excludes commercial use, so coverage depends on the app's period — offline, app on and waiting, or en route with a passenger. The rideshare carrier's contingent and full coverage attach to those periods.

Answer anchor — rideshare advantages and limits: higher limits while the trip is active, but slower handling, more documentation and a dispute over which period applied; the personal policy is faster but may exclude the loss entirely.

Answer anchor — dropped cases: the client must be notified in writing, promptly, with the reason and the statute implications, so they can seek other counsel in time. Delay is both an ethical breach and a malpractice exposure.
Answer anchor — automation: templates and reminders are appropriate for cadence and deadlines, never for substantive communication with a client or an adjuster.
pitfalls: Answers on rideshare that ignore the app-period distinction — that is the whole question.
Answers on dropped cases that treat notification as courtesy rather than obligation.

Q3: correct comparative liability reduction and its effect
Q4: names the app periods (offline / waiting / en route)
Q5: both advantages and limitations given
Q6: a line drawn between cadence and substance
Q7: written, prompt notification with reason and statute implications
nlp: Seven questions, equal weight, scored semantically against the answer anchors.
Q4 requires the app-period distinction for more than half marks.
Q7 requires the obligation framing: an answer that treats notification as optional courtesy caps at 25% of that item.

trainer.feedback: Which of the seven to revisit before the Day 12 demo…

v002.objective: The objective: what a Claims Specialist is responsible for.

v003.objective: The role in the early stages of a PI claim.
talk: Early means everything here: the claims opened in the first days decide what can be recovered later.

v004.objective: The workflow — read it as the map of Days 10 to 12.
talk: Determine coverage, open the claims, send the LOR, chase the policy and the liability decision.

v005.objective: Determining what coverage exists is the first critical task.
talk: No coverage found, no claim to open. This is detective work before it is paperwork.

v007.objective: Opening a claim accurately and efficiently.
talk: Accurately first. A wrong claim number costs more than a slow call.
Keep the pace up here; the sequence lands on the checklist page next.

v014.objective: Determine all insurance involved, then act on what is identified.
talk: Both sides, every vehicle, every potentially liable party.

v015.objective: Ask where and how to send supporting documents, and confirm it.
talk: Email, fax or portal — get it from the adjuster, not from assumption.

v017.objective: When a claim is already open.
talk: Take the existing number, confirm the adjuster, and do not open a duplicate.
pitfalls: Opening a second claim on the same loss. It confuses the carrier and delays everything.

v018.objective: Wrongful death at the pre-litigation stage.
talk: The claim is opened for the estate, which means the representative's authority has to be established first.

v019.objective: At litigation, the role expands to the estate and the heirs.

v020.objective: Claims on behalf of statutory heirs, who may also have personal claims.
talk: More claimants against one policy limit — which is the multiple-claimant conflict from the intake deck.

v021.objective: Open the Letter of Representation section.

v022.objective: The retainer agreement as the contract behind the LOR.
talk: The LOR is only truthful because the agreement exists. No signed agreement, no LOR.

v023.objective: What the LOR does: notify everyone that counsel represents the client.
talk: From that moment, contact goes through the firm. That is the whole point of sending it fast.

v025.objective: Premises liability: LOR and the preservation letter together.
talk: Footage is overwritten in days, so the preservation request is time-critical.

v026.objective: Dog bite: the letter goes to the owner; and where the incident happened matters.
talk: Homeowner's or renter's insurance is usually the policy in play.

v029.objective: The note to the carrier, and giving them a time frame.
talk: A stated deadline is what makes a follow-up possible.

v030.objective: The policy copy request and the evidence preservation request.
talk: Both go in the LOR as standard. Leaving either out means a second letter later.
keys: Every LOR asks for: a certified copy of the policy (the Dec Page) and preservation of any video or physical evidence.

v032.objective: The acknowledgment letter: the carrier confirms receipt.
talk: Diarise the follow-up from the date the LOR went out, not from the acknowledgment.

v033.objective: What the acknowledgment often gives you.
talk: Claim number, adjuster, and sometimes the disclosure statement. Record all of it in SA.

v034.objective: Statement of insurance disclosure, and that it varies by jurisdiction.
talk: Some states compel disclosure on request; others do not. Know which one the case is in.

v037.objective: The Dec Page as the blueprint of the policy.

v038.objective: Declarations page, sample — walk the fields, do not read them.

v041.objective: Insured vehicles: year, make, model, and whether our client's vehicle is on it.
talk: If the vehicle is not listed, ask why before assuming there is no coverage.

v042.objective: Deductibles: what the insured pays before the policy responds.

v044.objective: Comprehensive: theft, vandalism and other events outside the driver's control.

v046.objective: PIP / 1P coverage and limits, usually easy to obtain.
talk: Easy to get and often the first money into the file. Open it early.

v047.objective: Types of policy limits — the structures that follow.

v050.objective: CSL against per-person/per-accident, side by side.
talk: Have the room say which structure is better for a single badly injured claimant, and why.

v053.objective: The goal: get the BI carrier to accept liability.
talk: Everything in this section serves that one sentence.

v054.objective: Fault, and that the at-fault party holds legal responsibility.

talk: The carrier runs its own investigation. Our evidence is what it runs on.

v056.objective: The step-by-step table — read the steps, not the whole table.

v058.objective: What happens next: the case goes on hold while treatment continues.
talk: On hold is not idle — it is the records and bills stage.

v059.objective: The next step after acceptance: the demand.

v060.objective: Why acceptance matters to the file.

v061.objective: Get the acceptance in writing, every time.
talk: A verbal acceptance is not an acceptance. Ask for it by email.
keys: Once liability is admitted, obtain written confirmation and save it to the file.

v071.objective: Liability acceptance after a lawsuit is filed.

talk: Then close on the guide table.

v075.objective: Liability denied, coverage accepted — and what that combination means.
talk: Read it against the previous page: the two words move independently.

v001.objective: Open the Medical Records Specialist role: Days 13 to 17 run from this deck.
talk: Today is the discussion and the breakout plus the HIPAA certification task; Day 14 is the MedLOR demo; Day 16 is lien balance verification; Day 17 is saving the bills and records.
Say the two time limits now so nobody is surprised: 1 hour 45 minutes for the MedLOR demo, 45 minutes for the LV demo.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting Provider Communication — the Medical Records Specialist Role.

This deck carries Days 13 to 17: today's discussion, breakout and HIPAA certification, then your MedLOR demo, your Lien Balance Verification demo, and saving medical bills and records.

Two time limits to plan for:
• MedLOR demo — ideal completion 1 hour 45 minutes.
• LV request demo — ideal completion 45 minutes.

Going beyond either is a deduction under Time Management & Efficiency. Thank you.

keys: Tools to have working BEFORE the demos: Smart Advocate, Microsoft Word (for the templates), Notepad, and Nitro Pro or another PDF editor that can merge files and edit existing text.
A missed demo through unpreparedness is a missed performance and is NOT rescheduled. Only a Training Team factor justifies a reschedule.

v002.objective: The objective: request, organize and handle records accurately and ethically.

v003.objective: The agenda: introduction, legal compliance, providers and liens.

v004.objective: The role's place on the team, in PI cases.
talk: No records, no demand. This role controls the pace of the second half of every case.

v005.objective: What they will actually do: the bridge between the firm and the providers.
talk: Bridge, handler of confidential information, and chaser. All three are graded in the demos.

v006.objective: Open Protected Health Information — the section that carries the HIPAA task.

v007.objective: They handle the most confidential information in the case.
talk: Say it plainly: a PHI mistake is reportable, and it is the firm's liability, not just theirs.
Keep it practical — the test is whether they can say what they may and may not do with a record today.
Tonight's certification task covers the rest.
keys: HIPAA protects the privacy and security of identifiable health information. Our authority to hold it comes from the client's signed authorization, nothing else.

v009.objective: State privacy laws can be stricter than HIPAA.
talk: The rule is simple and worth memorising: follow the more restrictive of the two.
Encrypted email, the case portal, the CMS. Nothing else carries PHI.

v011.objective: What NOT to do — read every line aloud.
talk: No PHI on personal devices or personal email. No information to anyone not authorized.
This is the page that becomes a Process Question on the consequences of mishandling PHI.
keys: Consequences of mishandling PHI: civil and criminal penalties under HIPAA, state penalties, loss of the client's trust, sanctions against the firm, and dismissal for the VA.
pitfalls: Forwarding a record to a personal address 'to work on it at home'. That is the violation, by itself.

v012.objective: What PHI actually is: name, birthdate, contact, treatment, billing.
talk: If it identifies the person and touches their health or payment for it, it is PHI.
Secure systems, minimum necessary, verify the recipient, log what was sent.

v014.objective: Common HIPAA violations — the list they will be tested against.
talk: Wrong recipient, personal device or email, unsecured discussion, over-disclosure.
Ask the room which of these is easiest to do by accident. The answer is the wrong recipient on a fax.
keys: Before sending: verify the recipient's fax number or email twice, and attach the correct file — check the file, not the file name.
pitfalls: A transposed fax digit sends PHI to a stranger. Fill the recipient box LAST and verify it.

v015.objective: State privacy laws, in more detail.

v016.objective: The state-by-state table — point at the pattern, not every row.

v017.objective: Stricter consent requirements in some states.

v018.objective: Shorter response times in some states.
talk: This changes the follow-up cadence, which is what the demos are marked on.

v019.objective: Best practice: check the state, follow the more restrictive rule.
talk: Close the compliance section here; this is the line to carry into every provider call.

v020.objective: Open the Medical Records Request section — the core of the Day 14 demo.

v021.objective: Timeline and responsibility: once the agreement is signed, the firm requests.
talk: Tie it back to the intake packet: the signed HIPAA is what makes the request possible.

v022.objective: When requests should be made — and the older-DOL rule.
talk: An older date of loss means file as soon as possible; a fresh one follows treatment.
The PI Workflow deck's 4–8 week guide applies to a current DOL.
keys: Older DOL — request immediately, because the statute and the provider's own retention clock are both running.

v023.objective: The key check before requesting: treatment status, providers, dates of service.
talk: Dates of service drive the file naming on Day 17. Get them right at request time.

v024.objective: Request from ALL relevant providers to build a complete file.
talk: One missed provider understates the damages and can be fatal to the demand.

v025.objective: The PCP and referrals — always ask.
talk: Referrals are how the hidden providers surface.

v026.objective: The 14-day rule: confirm treatment within 14 days of the date of loss.
talk: Say why it matters — many policies and carriers treat a longer gap as a break in causation.
keys: Confirm treatment began within 14 days of the DOL. A longer gap must be flagged to the attorney with the reason, if the client gives one.
pitfalls: Recording 'no treatment' when the client went to an urgent care and forgot. Ask specifically.

v027.objective: The summary, including EMS: check for ambulance involvement and request those records.
talk: EMS records are the most commonly forgotten and the most useful for the first account of the injury.

v028.objective: Open the request checklist: forms, provider, drafting.

v029.objective: HIPAA authorization is the critical first step — confirm it before anything is requested.
talk: No valid authorization, no request. This is where a demo goes wrong in the first five minutes.
keys: On the HIPAA form: the Validity of Authorization date is the date the CLIENT SIGNED, as indicated below the document. Relationship to Patient is 'Self'.

v030.objective: The step-by-step: check the file, verify the signed forms.
talk: Walk it as a sequence they will narrate during the demo.

v031.objective: HITECH requests and signature requirements — some providers refuse the standard HIPAA form.

v032.objective: What to do when a provider requires a HITECH form: notify the client first.
talk: Notify, get it signed, then request. Never improvise a substitute form.

v033.objective: Identifying providers not listed at intake.

v034.objective: Ask the client, confirm where they went.
talk: Who authorizes contacting the client is firm policy. Check the SOP before dialling.

v035.objective: When providers refuse to confirm details.
talk: This is the page the Day 15 communication upskill is built on: assertive, polite, persistent.
Escalate after two failed attempts, with the attempts logged.
keys: A provider who will not confirm: send the authorization again, ask for the records department by name, log each attempt with date and time, and escalate after two failures.

v036.objective: Quick care, urgent care, and the Certificate of No Records.
talk: The certificate is itself a document for the file — it proves the gap was checked.
Different route, same paperwork. Know which department.

v038.objective: Drafting the MedLOR — and the naming convention the Day 14 demo is marked on.
talk: Tick the correct box for bills, records, or both, matching what the request actually asks for.
Then give the naming convention and the NPIM variant, because both are scored.
keys: MED - Lien Holder(Medical Provider) - MedLOR with Unsworn COR and HIPAA mm.dd.yy (va's first name)
Example: MED - JML(Lyons Physical Therapy) - MedLOR with Unsworn COR and HIPAA 08.11.22 (John)
NPIM providers: always add the doctor's name — MED - JML(Fabito Anesthesia Pain Center Dr. Fabito) - MedLOR with Unsworn COR and HIPAA 08.11.22 (John)
Email subject: [Client Name] - [Lien Holder] - Request for Medical Bills and Records

SA update: the MEDS tab is under the GENERAL section now, not Plaintiff. For the DOCGEN dummy account use the client name John Test Doe in the documents, but take every other detail from the CURRENT contact card (which shows 'I Test Doe').
pitfalls: Ticking both bills and records when the task asks for one.
Copying the client's details from the tutorial video instead of the current contact card.
Looking for the MEDS tab under Plaintiff and losing demo minutes to it.

grade.file: MED - Lien Holder(Medical Provider) - MedLOR with Unsworn COR and HIPAA mm.dd.yy (va's first name)

match: File name matches the convention exactly, including the doctor's name for an NPIM provider
HIPAA validity date equals the client's signature date; relationship is 'Self'
Correct request box ticked (bills / records / both)
Client details match the current contact card, not the tutorial video
Document uploaded: Direction Outgoing, sub-category Medical/meds, folder Meds, FROM OUR FIRM, TO the provider
Copy attached in the MEDS tab under GENERAL, and in the Tasks tab
Notes and Tasks reports use the templates, with the internal link hyperlinked
Fax address formatted +1XXXXXXXXXX@metrofax.com with no dashes
Completed within 1 hour 45 minutes
nlp: The file name is parsed field by field — provider, document set, date format mm.dd.yy, and the VA's first name in parentheses; a wrong date format is a failed field, not a typo.
Report templates are matched semantically but the required phrases 'Saved in Meds and Docs tab' and 'Thank you' must be present.
Time over 1 hour 45 minutes is scored as a deduction against Time Management & Efficiency, not against accuracy.

scores.label: SA workflow — upload, MEDS, Notes, Tasks

rubric: Narrated the verification steps rather than clicking silently
Prepared — tools working before the demo started
Returned 5–10 minutes later to check the transmission confirmation
trainer.feedback: Where the time went, and which SA step needs a second pass…

v039.objective: The SOAP note format — how to read what comes back.
talk: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan. Knowing it is how they spot a record that is incomplete.

v040.objective: Prepare the documents before sending: MedLOR, HIPAA, COR.
talk: Everything merged into one combined file before it goes. Nitro Pro is what they merge with.
keys: The combined document is what gets uploaded and sent: MedLOR + Unsworn Certificate of Records + HIPAA.

v041.objective: E-portals: check the provider's location first.
talk: Right portal, right facility. A request to the wrong location is a lost week.
A follow-up without a logged previous attempt is not a follow-up.

v043.objective: Document review and file organization on receipt.
talk: Check what arrived against what was asked for, before reporting it received.
keys: Day 17 naming for what comes back: MED - Provider - HICF $0.00 & Records DOS mm.dd.yy with Signed COR and Unsigned Lien (va's first name), then the bill, records and lien named separately when extracted.

v044.objective: Notate everything, and back up before editing.
talk: Every call, every action, in the system. The note is the proof the work happened.

v045.objective: The pre-send checklist: full name, DOB, dates of service.
talk: Run it as a checklist in the demo, out loud. It is marked.
keys: Before sending: client's full name and DOB present, dates of service specified, authorization attached and valid, recipient verified.

v046.objective: Sending the request — the checklist's send step.

v047.objective: After sending: confirm transmission, log it, diarise the follow-up.
talk: Return 5–10 minutes later for the transmission confirmation. If it failed, resend until it confirms.

v048.objective: Upon receiving the documents: check, name, save, report.

v049.objective: Open Lien Balance Verification — the Day 16 demo.
talk: Name the 45-minute target now.

v050.objective: Mid-treatment lien balance verification, and why LOPs matter.
talk: LOPs are legally binding; mismanaging one delays the settlement.
This is the Process Question on liens versus LOPs, and the one on why lien accuracy matters.
keys: Medical lien — a legal claim against the settlement proceeds, often statutory or contractual.
Letter of Protection (LOP) — the firm's written promise to pay the provider from the settlement, so treatment continues without the client paying up front.
Both reduce the client's net, and both must be verified before any net sheet is built.

v051.objective: The purpose: keep bills within policy limits, spot excess.
talk: Bills above the policy limit is the problem the Lien Negotiator inherits. Catching it mid-treatment is the whole point.

v052.objective: When to check: 30–45 days into active treatment, and after any major procedure.

v053.objective: How to do it: list every active provider, including imaging and specialists.
talk: Then give the Day 16 naming and templates, because the demo is marked on them.
keys: MED – Lien Holder(Provider) – Lien Balance Verification mm.dd.yyyy (va's first name)
NPIM: MED - RDG(NPIM Dr. Fabito) - Lien Balance Verification 08.17.2022 (jane)
Notes tab: Sent [filename without the VA's name]. Saved in Meds and Docs tab. Thank you. (va's first name) — highlight the file name and paste the internal link.
Tasks tab: mm/dd/yyyy Sent LV request to [lien holder(medical provider)]. Saved in Meds and Docs tab. Thank you. (va's first name)
Email subject: [Client Name] - [Lien Holder] - Request for Lien Verification
Ideal completion time: 45 minutes. Overruns are heavily penalised.
pitfalls: Using mm.dd.yy instead of mm.dd.yyyy — the LV convention uses the four-digit year.
Leaving the VA's name in the file name quoted inside the Notes report.

grade.file: MED – Lien Holder(Provider) – Lien Balance Verification mm.dd.yyyy (va's first name)

match: File name matches the convention, with the four-digit year and the NPIM doctor where applicable
Upload properties: Outgoing, Medical/meds, folder Meds, FROM OUR FIRM, TO the provider
Copy attached in the Meds tab and the Tasks tab
Notes report matches the template, with the internal link on the file name
Tasks report matches the template, dated mm/dd/yyyy
Email subject matches [Client Name] - [Lien Holder] - Request for Lien Verification
Completed within 45 minutes
nlp: Check the Notes report excludes the VA's name from the quoted file name but signs with it at the end — that is the most commonly failed field.
Date formats are exact: mm.dd.yyyy in the file name, mm/dd/yyyy in the Tasks report.
Time beyond 45 minutes is scored against Time Management & Efficiency only.

rubric: Worked from their own process guide
trainer.feedback: Which field cost them, and whether the 45 minutes was realistic for them…

talk: Post the four handouts, run the five Priority questions, then the Document Detectives exercise.
Set the HIPAA certification task with the naming rule and the screenshot requirement — the timestamp must be visible.

gc.text:
PROCESS QUESTIONS

1. Evaluate the impact of delayed or missing records on the ability to prepare a strong demand letter or settlement package.
2. Evaluate the consequences of mishandling PHI in a legal setting. What are the ethical, legal, and financial implications?
3. Analyze the difference between medical liens and letters of protection. How do both impact case settlement?
4. Evaluate the role of the Legal VA in tracking and communicating lien balances. Why is accuracy critical in lien resolution?
5. Analyze the difference between medical bills, treatment records, diagnostic reports, and discharge summaries. What role does each play in a demand letter?

Save your answers in your Assessments/Activities folder as:
Medical_Records_Specialist_Training_Process_Question_Answers_[your first name]

Type "done" here once uploaded. Thank you.

gc.text:
Please proceed to watch the tutorial video on Sending MedLOR and Requesting Medical Bills & Records.

https://drive.google.com/file/d/16Oy2X1S9nokz5tqMm_P6nByqYaakvGDU/view

NOTE: While watching, create your own notes or work guide so you have something to refer to during your recorded demonstration. Please SKIP the segment from 58:12 to 58:45. Thank you.

keys: Full list is 10 questions; the Priority track is the 5 above.
Answer anchor — delayed records: no records means no demand, so the statute runs while the file waits; an incomplete package understates damages and invites a low offer.

Answer anchor — lien accuracy: the lien balance sets the client's net, so an error either shorts the client or exposes the firm to a provider's claim after disbursement; it must match the provider's own figure in writing.
Answer anchor — document roles: bills prove the amount, treatment records prove causation and course, diagnostic reports prove the injury objectively, discharge summaries prove severity and the plan.
HIPAA certificate naming: HIPAA Certificate_[Your Name], screenshot with a visible timestamp, DM'd to Michelle.
pitfalls: Screenshots without a visible timestamp — they are not accepted as proof.
Watching the Day 14 tutorial without building the process guide, then losing demo minutes to it.
